fieldData.excerpt: Someone was awake before us every morning, making the coffee. That, more than the summit, is what I brought down the mountain.
fieldData.body:
Most mornings began the same way: cold toes, frosted breath, and a warm aluminum cup of Tanzanian coffee delivered quietly to the tent.

It was simple. It was sacred. And it meant that before we had unzipped anything, before we had locked eyes with the beautiful beast that is Kilimanjaro, someone else had already been awake for an hour making it.

That is the part I keep coming back to. Not the summit. The coffee.

We did not conquer anything

Eight days on the Lemosho Route with Much Better Adventures and the team from Ahsante Tours. Nine hikers. Twenty-eight crew.

Sit with that ratio for a second, because it is the real story of this mountain and almost nobody tells it. For every one of us walking up with a daypack, there were three people carrying the tents, the food, the water, the kitchen, and the toilets, moving faster than us, usually past us, often singing.

There is an organization called the Kilimanjaro Porters Assistance Project that exists because this ratio has historically been easy to abuse. Their standard is that a porter's load should not exceed 20 kilograms on top of his own kit, that he should get three adequate meals a day, proper shelter and sleeping gear, and care if he gets sick or hurt, and that he should be paid at least the Tanzanian minimum wage within two days of coming down. None of that is exotic. All of it has to be said out loud, which tells you something.

So if you go: ask your operator where they stand on this before you book, not after. Ask how many crew, ask what the tipping procedure is, and ask for it in writing. We did not conquer the mountain. We were carried up it by people who were very good at their jobs, and the least you can do is know their terms of employment.

Team Sexy Awesome

Nine of us. Five Americans, three Brits, and one beloved Tanzanian teammate named Melvin, going for his first summit.

We named ourselves Team Sexy Awesome. Obviously.

Alan, king of washy-washy, boisterous and affectionate, lit up the mess tent and the trail. A quiet Alan was a cause for concern. We called him The Honey Badger, because he took on the rules the way one does, which is to say not at all. Fittingly, Jay and I later saw an actual honey badger on our post-trek safari.

Nicole, full of warmth and wisdom, brought the quiet can-do calm, and grounded Alan in the best possible way.

Tom, also known as The Count, counted out loud at random with deep commitment. For science? For vibes? Never established. He could also be heard singing in the loo and recounting vivid dreams about washing his car.

Sarah, a doctor, dispensed mountain medical advice with the authority of a saint. But it was the Mars Bar that told you that you had made the inner circle.

Charlotte is living in Tanzania teaching business for a while. She led our stretchy-stretchy routines with Cha Cha Slide energy and was rumored to be sitting on a private supply of the good peanut butter.

Emily introduced us to the hot water Nalgene trick, which Jay had fully stolen by the last day. She also brought the most nostalgic playlist in existence for the long cold hours, and won the local team over with Jolly Ranchers.

Melvin was the youngest and the bougiest of us, and would switch into Swahili when he wanted extra pampering from the crew. We were on to him. Summit day was the first time he had ever seen snow, and the first time he learned what it actually does to your hands.

And us. Jay crab-walked into the tent more than once. I apparently muttered "gross" while sleep-snuggling, our first camping trip as a couple, which means the unshowered stench made it all the way into my dreams.

The numbers

  • Days on trail: 8
  • Highest point: 5,895 meters
  • Flush toilet tents: 2
  • Number of Kevins in our group: 0, though we were assured he existed
  • Uno games lost to the crew: painful

How it actually went

Day 1. Moshi. Kilimanjaro beer. Fruit markets, and an avocado I still think about. Coffee tastings. Happy birthday, Alan.

Day 2. We sing into the forest. No cell service. We chase skunky monkeys. We are the playlist.

Days 3 to 5. Clear the tree line. WiFi at Lizard Rock, of all places, and porters scrolling on their phones in the sun with an ocean of cloud behind them. Across the Shira Plateau. Up through Lava Tower and into the altitude-induced silence.

Day 6. The Barranco Wall. Made out with the Kissing Rock. Braved what we named Kama Sutra Pass, and no, don't ask.

Day 7. Rest, pack, hydrate. Watch Jay enter the tent like a man who lost a fight with gravity. Early night, warmed by drinking chocolate.

Summit night

Cold. Quiet. A very long think, broken only by the crew's chants of "more fire, more water" as we climbed into the sky.

We reached Uhuru Peak at a bright orange sunrise. My fingers were ice. The view was worth every one of them.

And here is the thing nobody photographs properly. That sign, the wide-angle one in every advertisement in town, is cute. It is not the story. The story is up and to the left: glassy, jagged, silent fields of ice, sharp shelves of it standing in the open like walls, and a crater view that does not fit in a frame.

Look at them while you can. In November 2022 UNESCO and the IUCN published a report finding that glaciers in a third of the fifty World Heritage sites that have them will disappear by 2050 no matter what anyone does now. Every glacier in an African World Heritage site is on that list. Kilimanjaro is on that list.

The ice I stood next to at sunrise is scheduled to be gone within my lifetime, and the sign at the top will still be there, and the photographs in the shop windows in Moshi will still show the white summit, and that is a strange thing to carry down a mountain.

We hugged. We scree-skied back down the gravel with legs like overcooked spaghetti. We were rewarded with chairs and Tang, which at that moment was the finest beverage ever devised.

Coming down

On the last day Melvin sprinted through the jungle in a neon poncho like a SpongeBob-quoting starfish.

We skipped through puddles and ferns and rain. The trail started to feel like home: moss, mud, and the sound of water.

That night we watched acrobats limbo under fire. A contortionist nearly gave Sarah a full panic attack, and we learned she is considerably more afraid of spider-shaped humans than of actual spiders. We swam. We toasted. We ate. We slept like bricks.

To the people who made it possible

To Musa, The Professor, and Eddie: asante. You led with humor and knowledge and care. You sang, you coached, and you held the mountain steady for us.

To the twenty-eight: you showed up for us before we knew what we needed. You cleaned our boots, brought popcorn, hauled the tents, and cheered every single step.

Next time: more socks, fewer clothes, face masks for a tent-side spa night, and considerably more Mars Bars.

This was not just a trek. It was trust. It was laughter at altitude. It was holding each other up through desert and steep walls and sleep-muttered snuggles.

To anyone dreaming about this mountain: say yes. You will come home changed. That is the whole point.

And someone will already be awake, making your coffee. Learn his name.

P.S. Narwhal!

fieldData.short-version: Nancy Carleton and her husband Jay climbed Mount Kilimanjaro by the Lemosho Route over eight days in August 2025, reaching Uhuru Peak at 5,895 meters, with Much Better Adventures and the Tanzanian operator Ahsante Tours. Their group was nine hikers supported by twenty-eight crew, a ratio she argues is the real and under-told story of the mountain: the Kilimanjaro Porters Assistance Project sets standards of a 20 kilogram maximum load per porter excluding his own kit, three meals a day, proper shelter and gear, and payment of at least the Tanzanian minimum wage within two days of descent. At the summit she found the glaciers more striking than the famous sign, and a 2022 UNESCO and IUCN report finds that Kilimanjaro's glaciers, along with those at every African World Heritage site, will very likely be gone by 2050. Reported first-hand for That Layover Life.
fieldData.quick-answers:
How long does the Lemosho Route take?

This trek was eight days on the trail, summiting at Uhuru Peak, 5,895 meters. Lemosho approaches from the west and crosses the Shira Plateau, which gives more time to acclimatize than the shorter routes.

How many porters and crew does a Kilimanjaro climb use?

On this trip, nine hikers were supported by twenty-eight crew, roughly three crew per client. That is normal. The crew carry tents, food, water, the kitchen and the toilets, and typically move faster than the clients.

What are the standards for porter treatment on Kilimanjaro?

The Kilimanjaro Porters Assistance Project sets out that a porter's load for the company should not exceed 20 kilograms on top of his own kit, that he should receive three adequate meals a day, proper shelter, sleeping equipment and gear, care if sick or injured, and at least the Tanzanian minimum wage paid within two days of descent. They also advise asking your operator for the crew count and the tipping procedure in advance, to avoid extra people appearing at the tipping ceremony to claim a share.

Are the glaciers on Kilimanjaro disappearing?

Yes. In November 2022 UNESCO and the IUCN published World Heritage Glaciers: Sentinels of Climate Change, which found that glaciers at a third of the fifty World Heritage sites that have them will disappear by 2050 regardless of emissions action, and that glaciers at every African World Heritage site, Kilimanjaro National Park included, will very likely be gone by then.

How high is Uhuru Peak?

5,895 meters above sea level, which is the figure on the summit sign and the standard published height. It is the highest point in Africa.

fieldData.excerpt: Most of the world knows two words about Kazakhstan. Here is a canyon nobody mentions, a lake with a forest standing up inside it, and the supermarket aisle where I had no business at all.
fieldData.body:
In true "Nancy adds a layover nowhere near the way home" fashion, Jay and I flew back from Africa to Brazil by way of Kazakhstan.

We blame Ainura and Mati, and their extended family, who are the kind of friends you say yes to before you have looked at a map.

The two words problem

Most of the world knows exactly two words about Kazakhstan, and a British comedian in a gray suit put them there.

Here is the part that makes me like this country more, not less: in October 2020, Kazakh Tourism looked at that and decided not to fight it. They made "Very nice!" the official tourism slogan. The campaign came from an American living in Kazakhstan, and the pitch was more or less: people arrive expecting a punchline, and then they see the place.

That is a confident thing for a country to do. It is also, I can now report, accurate and badly incomplete.

Charyn: the canyon nobody mentions

Charyn is red rock stacked in layers, towers and walls and spires, running on past the point where your eye gives up. The section everyone photographs is called the Valley of Castles, and the name is not doing any work it does not need to do. They look like castles. A dirt road runs between them. You walk in, and the walls go up, and the sound of everything else goes away.

If you have been to the American Southwest, your brain will try to file this under Utah. Let it try. The light is different, the scale is different, and there is nobody there.

The lake with a forest standing in it

This is the one I keep describing to people, badly, at dinner parties.

Lake Kaindy is a narrow green lake in the Kungey Alatau with the trunks of dead spruce trees standing straight up out of the water, bare and pale, like masts.

Here is how that happens. In January 1911 an enormous earthquake hit the northern Tien Shan. It tore roughly 190 kilometers of surface ruptures across the mountains and killed 452 people. One of the things it did, along the way, was knock a mass of rock down into a gorge, which dammed the stream at the bottom of it.

The water backed up. It backed up into a spruce forest and kept rising, and the trees drowned where they stood.

What makes it strange rather than merely sad is that the trunks are still there, more than a century on. The water is glacial meltwater, cold enough and still enough that the wood has not rotted the way it would anywhere warmer. Below the surface the branches are reportedly still attached. Above it, the trees are bleached white and perfectly vertical, which is not a shape water usually leaves things in.

A forest did not fall into a lake. A lake rose into a forest, and the forest has been standing in it ever since.

If you go: base yourself in the village of Saty, about four to five hours from Almaty by road. The lower Kolsai lake sits at roughly 1,800 meters and is about ten kilometers on from Saty. Kaindy is in the next valley over, around eleven kilometers from the village, and the last stretch is a track rather than a road. You want four-wheel drive and you want to not be in a hurry.

Chai, which means tea

Not chai tea. Chai. Чай. The word is just tea, and ordering a "chai tea" here would get you the same look it gets you anywhere, which is to say you have asked for a tea tea.

It arrives hot, out of ornate metal urns, in the middle of a table with more on it than anyone could eat. At one stop there were falcons nearby and winter robes you could try on between sips, which is a sentence I did not expect to write about an afternoon drink.

The yurt, the dombra, and the Chileans

We slept in the coziest yurt of our lives. Felt walls, tassels, a painted round table, and a door that opens onto a mountain.

Dinner was dumplings, cookies, and the dried bread rusks everyone kept handing me that I will go to my grave calling croutons. Then marshmallows over the fire, and somebody playing a dombra.

The dombra is a two-stringed lute with a pear-shaped body and a long neck, and the short solo pieces played on it are called kuys. UNESCO put the art of the dombra kuy on its Representative List in 2014, partly because a kuy is rarely only music: it usually comes with the story or the legend attached to it, and it gets played at gatherings exactly like the one I was sitting in. I did not understand a word of the story. I understood the room.

Mati's Chilean family made piscolas, because of course they did.

The Bukhanka

The next morning we folded ourselves into a Soviet-era UAZ van, the kind with the flat face and the square body that Russians nicknamed the bukhanka, meaning loaf of bread, because it looks like one. They have been building essentially this same vehicle since the 1960s.

It has no modern safety features to speak of and a sound system playing Russian dance music at a volume that suggested the driver considered it structural. We went through potholes, through streams, up hillsides that did not look like roads because they were not roads. It was magnificent. Fresh watermelon from a stall on the way home, scooped out by hand.

The aisle where I had no business

Back in Almaty we had cocktails high above the city with the Zailiysky Alatau filling an entire wall of window. Mine arrived in a pufferfish. I have no further notes on the pufferfish.

Then a proper Kazakh feast: camel milk, horse for the adventurous at the table, and for me, hand-pulled noodles good enough that I thought about them on the flight home.

Which brings us to the grocery store.

Ainura was our primary translator and the only reason any of us knew what was happening at any given moment. She had to step away for a medical emergency. Which is how I, the pescatarian, got sent to the supermarket with the boys to buy steak.

Nobody working there spoke English. Nobody in our group spoke Kazakh or Russian. So we did the only thing available to us, which was to pick up a package of meat, hold it steady, photograph it, wait for Google to tell us what it was, and then put it back down. We would get a confident read on cow. It would turn out to be horse. Or camel.

Partway through this, Mati appeared holding something baguette-shaped and asked whether it was bread. He had come from a refrigerator in the pet food section. We relocated to the bakery and stayed in the bakery.

And then Tommy went missing.

Tommy is the tallest brother. This was a store with short shelves, the kind where you can see the entire floor from the entrance, which meant there was nowhere in the building a man of his height could possibly be. We found him fifteen minutes later, crouched down at the far end with his face almost on the floor, trying to read the label on a bottle of wine on the bottom shelf.

I am a pescatarian. I was the translator. Cultural barbecue diplomacy at its finest.

What I would tell you

Go for the people. We did, and everything else was a bonus that happened to include a canyon and a drowned forest.

Say yes to the van. Modern safety features are overrated and Russian dance music is underrated.

And drop the two words. Not because they are offensive, exactly, and clearly not because Kazakhstan is precious about them. Drop them because they take up the space where a real country should be, and this one turns out to be enormous, strange, generous, and full of people who will feed you until you stop being a guest.

Very nice, yes. And so much more.

P.S. A note of consideration, courtesy of a national park sign: don't garbage your grandchildren.

fieldData.short-version: Kazakhstan is best known abroad for a comedian's catchphrase, and in October 2020 the national tourism board made that catchphrase, "Very nice!", its official slogan. The country's draws include Charyn Canyon, whose Valley of Castles is a run of red rock towers and walls, and Lake Kaindy, where the trunks of a spruce forest drowned after a 1911 earthquake still stand upright in the water. fieldData.quick-answers:
Why is "Very nice!" Kazakhstan's tourism slogan?

Kazakh Tourism adopted the Borat catchphrase as its official slogan in October 2020, timed to the release of the second film. The campaign was conceived by an American living in Kazakhstan, on the logic that visitors arrive expecting a punchline and then see the country.

Why are there dead trees standing upright in Lake Kaindy?

A major earthquake struck the northern Tien Shan in January 1911, tearing roughly 190 kilometers of surface ruptures across the mountains. It brought down rock that dammed a gorge, and the rising water flooded a spruce forest. The cold glacial meltwater has preserved the trunks, which still stand vertically more than a century later.

How do you reach Lake Kaindy and the Kolsai lakes?

Base yourself in the village of Saty, roughly four to five hours by road from Almaty. The lower Kolsai lake is about ten kilometers on from Saty, at roughly 1,800 meters. Lake Kaindy is in the next valley, around eleven kilometers from the village, on a track that needs four-wheel drive.

What is a dombra?

A two-stringed Kazakh lute with a pear-shaped body and a long neck, played by plucking. The short solo pieces played on it are called kuys, and UNESCO added the Kazakh traditional art of Dombra Kuy to its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2014.

What is a bukhanka?

The nickname for the UAZ-452 van, meaning loaf of bread, after its shape. Essentially the same vehicle has been built since the 1960s and it is still a common way to reach roadless country in Kazakhstan.

fieldData.excerpt: I went to the Pantanal looking for small flashes of joy and came back with a jaguar doing zoomies, a hat that said something I did not intend, and the lingering smell of a very large stork.
fieldData.body:
There is a word going around for the small flashes of joy that show up even when everything else is a mess. Glimmers. I went looking for a few and came back with a jaguar, a linguistic disaster involving a hat, and the smell of a stork that has not entirely left me.

The Pantanal is the largest tropical wetland on earth. Most of it sits in Mato Grosso do Sul, but the part everyone photographs, the part with the road and the jaguars, is up in Mato Grosso. Embrapa's revised checklist puts 470 bird species on the floodplain, which is a lot of birds, and a good number of them look like they were designed by a committee that had been left alone with the coffee.

Almost everyone who goes does it the same way: a week-long guided safari, a lodge, a tracker, sundowners at golden hour, a lens the size of a fire extinguisher. Sami and I drove.

Sami is a historian, a fantasy author, and the best road snack strategist I have ever shared a car with. Neither of us had done this before. Neither, it turns out, had many people, which we learned gradually from the faces of everyone we met along the way.

Day one: red lightning and the long nothing

Eighteen hours of highway out of São Paulo. Tolls, soy fields that go past the horizon in every direction, and roadside statues so large and so unexplained that they felt like the Corn Palace having a fever dream.

Red lightning cracked across the sky somewhere in the dark while Welcome to Night Vale played through the speakers, which is either perfect or a warning, and I have decided it was perfect. Carlos would have approved.

Zebu cattle with their shoulder humps strolled the verge like they had somewhere better to be. Rheas, which are essentially emus with fewer career prospects, sprinted off through the tall grass. We passed a sign for a town called Coxim and both said it out loud at the same time, for reasons I will not be defending here.

We collapsed in Rondonópolis, which by then we were calling Ridonculous, delirious and extremely pleased with ourselves.

The road that ends on purpose

The Transpantaneira runs 147 kilometers from Poconé to Porto Jofre, and it crosses about 120 wooden bridges on the way.

That number is the whole personality of the road. It was drawn up in the 1970s, and the plan to pave it was abandoned to protect the wetland, so what got built instead was a raised dirt causeway with water on both sides and bridges spaced along it to let the floodwater pass underneath during the wet season. Then it simply stopped at Porto Jofre, where it still stops.

The result is the best wildlife corridor in South America, arrived at mostly by accident. Everything that lives in the water comes to the edges. The road is at the edge. You drive at twenty kilometers an hour and the Pantanal arranges itself along your window.

The bridges are wooden, individually numbered, and in widely varying states of opinion about your vehicle. You slow down for each one. One hundred and twenty times.

Before we started it, we stopped at the Cuiabá market for mystery snacks and a hat. More on the hat.

Kilometer 42

At Pousada Rio Claro we found tired mama monkeys hauling babies through the treetops, jabirus posing like they were being paid by the hour, and one capybara who came to our door and knocked. Not metaphorically. It wanted friendship and would not be rushed.

An old man walked past with a bucket, and a jabiru followed him at a respectful distance in what appeared to be an ongoing dispute about union benefits, the benefit in question being fish.

Jabirus, for the record, deserve the attention they give themselves. They are the tallest flying bird in the Americas, standing up to about five feet, with a wingspan that can reach nine. Remember this. It becomes relevant.

The pousada staff looked politely baffled that we had driven here ourselves. I assumed the bafflement was about the driving.

The hat

At the market I had bought a cap reading "Xô Cesso," which Google Translate had assured me meant something like "shoo, mosquito." Practical. Thematic. I wore it all afternoon through a crowded market, pleased with my own cultural integration.

Later, someone kindly took me aside and explained that the phrase does not refer to mosquitoes. It refers, with some specificity, to male anatomy.

So I had spent an entire afternoon walking around northern Mato Grosso wearing a hat that politely requested every man in the vicinity keep his anatomy at a respectful distance. To the tourists: sensible insect advice. To everyone who actually speaks Portuguese: a woman making a very bold opening statement.

I have never been prouder of a purchase.

Why the jaguars let you watch

Here is the thing about Porto Jofre that nobody tells you until you are already in the boat.

Jaguars are famously impossible to see. People spend years in the Amazon and never manage it, and researchers estimate that jaguars can reliably be seen in less than five percent of the range the species still occupies. And yet here, on this one floodplain where the Cuiabá River braids out into a hundred channels, you can reasonably expect to.

I had assumed this was about the dry season pushing prey onto the riverbanks. That is part of it, and season does show up in the models. But it is not the main thing, and the main thing is better.

In the 1960s and 1980s, poaching had very nearly wiped jaguars out of this region. What has happened since is a slow recovery, and alongside it something stranger: the cats have decided we are furniture. The Jaguar ID Project counted 29 habituated jaguars here in 2013. By 2023 it counted 130. That is not 130 more jaguars appearing from nowhere. That is 130 individual animals who have independently concluded that a boat is a boring and harmless feature of the river.

So the honest version is this. The jaguars are visible because people stopped shooting them, and because enough generations have now grown up with boats drifting past that watching one no longer costs it anything. That is the whole mechanism, and it took forty years.

It is also, now, worth money. Jaguar tourism here generates an estimated 6.8 million US dollars a year, which is the argument that keeps the cats alive in a landscape otherwise given over to cattle. And it is under strain. Researchers counted roughly four boats a day on the river in low season and around thirty in high season, and a 2025 study argued the whole thing needs new rules before it collapses under its own popularity.

We went in October, which is high season. We found that out from behind.

Our first jaguar was asleep and so motionless that we spent a genuinely long time debating whether he was taxidermied. He was not. He was just extremely comfortable.

Then, further down the river, we were the first boat to find one moving: a golden shadow cutting a line through the current, swimming. We had fifteen minutes alone with him before the other boats found us and queued up behind, the photographers with the enormous lenses and, inexplicably, a group of shirtless frat boys. The jaguar swam, climbed out, strutted the bank, pooped with great ceremony, and did a lap of what I can only describe as zoomies. Fifteen minutes of a wild apex predator auditioning for Dancing with the Predators.

A heron caught a fish, dropped it theatrically, and then looked directly at me for applause.

We also beached our boat on a submerged log at a forty-five degree angle in a stretch our guide cheerfully called Caiman Alley, and spent roughly thirty seconds doing math about our odds while the caimans watched with what I would characterize as interest. Another boat pulled us off.

The stork, concluded

On the drive back down the Transpantaneira, with the windows open, a jabiru passed overhead and delivered directly into the car.

My arm. The windshield. A substantial quantity.

Recall that this is a bird standing five feet tall whose diet runs to fish, frogs, snakes, snails and, when the season turns hard, whatever has already died. The scent profile was exactly what that sentence implies. We laughed until we could not see, which is a poor condition for driving, and then we bought an air freshener.

No giant anteater. No giant otter. Those were the two I wanted most and the Pantanal declined to provide them.

Chapada, and down

We came off the road into Chapada dos Guimarães at sunset, red rock and canyon, and the hotel we had booked on points turned out to be genuinely beautiful. Purple sky, limoncello spritz, fresh fish.

Morning was bananas with cinnamon and dulce de leche, which I recommend as a way of being alive. Then the Morro do Vento overlook, red cliffs in gold light, and a search for a waterfall that Google Maps had invented. The dirt road ended instead at a vegetarian restaurant in the middle of the jungle. No regrets at all.

Then Campo Grande, where the hotel staff greeted us in flawless English learned entirely from Call of Duty. Then pig statues, unexplained farm smells, and Três Lagoas, which lived up to its name only barely.

What I would tell you

You can do this without a guide. We did. But be honest with yourself about which parts you are actually doing alone, because we were not: we drove ourselves and booked ourselves, and then we got in a boat with a man who knew exactly where the jaguars were. The driving is the DIY part. The jaguars are not.

Track your fuel like you are running a space program. Gas stations vanish for hours at a time on the Transpantaneira and do not come back until you have driven the whole thing and returned.

Go in the dry season, roughly June through October. Go late in it if you can stand the company, and know that in high season you are one of about thirty boats and the etiquette matters: engines off, keep your distance, and do not ask your guide to push in.

Drive it slowly. Twenty kilometers an hour is not a limitation, it is the entire product.

And this is the part I actually came back with. I went looking for glimmers, which is a small and manageable ambition, the kind you set when you are tired. What I got was a week of them stacked end to end: lightning, a capybara at the door, a terrible hat, a jaguar doing zoomies, a bird emptying itself into my car. Joy did not arrive quietly on this trip. It arrived at volume, slightly damp, and smelling strongly of stork.

fieldData.short-version: The Transpantaneira is a 147 km raised dirt road running from Poconé to Porto Jofre through the northern Pantanal in Mato Grosso, crossing about 120 wooden bridges. It was drawn up in the 1970s; the plan to pave it was dropped to protect the wetland, and it dead-ends at Porto Jofre. It can be driven in an ordinary car and makes an effective wildlife corridor, because the causeway sits at the water's edge. Porto Jofre is the most reliable place on earth to see wild jaguars, and the main reason is not the dry season but recovery and habituation: poaching had nearly eliminated jaguars from the region by the 1980s, and the Jaguar ID Project counted 29 habituated individuals in 2013 against 130 in 2023. Jaguars can be reliably seen in under five percent of the species' remaining range. Jaguar tourism here is valued at roughly US$6.8 million a year, and boat traffic rises from about four a day in low season to around thirty in high season, which researchers warn is unsustainable without new rules. We drove from São Paulo in October 2025, self-organized, and hired a boat and guide at Porto Jofre.
fieldData.quick-answers:
How long is the Transpantaneira and how many bridges does it have?

147 kilometers, from Poconé to Porto Jofre in Mato Grosso, crossing about 120 wooden bridges. It is dirt, raised on an embankment, and it dead-ends at Porto Jofre.

Can you drive the Transpantaneira in a normal car?

Yes, in the dry season. We did it in a standard rental. Drive slowly, take the wooden bridges one at a time, and plan fuel carefully, because there are no gas stations along the road itself.

Do you need a guide to visit the Pantanal?

Not for the driving, the lodges or the road itself, all of which you can arrange yourself. You do need a boat and a local guide to see jaguars at Porto Jofre, and that part is not worth improvising.

Why can you see jaguars at Porto Jofre when they are invisible everywhere else?

Mainly because the population recovered after poaching nearly eliminated it, and because the cats have become habituated to boats over decades. The Jaguar ID Project counted 29 habituated jaguars in 2013 and 130 in 2023. Season, river proximity and weather also affect sighting odds, but habituation is the core of it. Jaguars can be reliably seen in less than five percent of their remaining range.

When is the best time to see jaguars in the Pantanal?

The dry season, roughly June through October. Water levels drop, access improves and sighting rates are at their highest.

How crowded does it get?

Researchers recorded roughly four boats a day on the river in low season and around thirty in high season. A 2025 study argued that jaguar tourism here needs new rules to stay sustainable. In high season expect to share a sighting and to queue.

How many bird species live in the Pantanal?

Embrapa's revised checklist for the Pantanal floodplain records 470 species.

What is a jabiru?

A very large wetland stork, the tallest flying bird in the Americas, standing up to about five feet with a wingspan reaching nine. They are common along the Transpantaneira.

How do you get to the Pantanal from São Paulo?

Fly to Cuiabá and drive south, or do what we did and drive the whole way, which is about eighteen hours to Rondonópolis on the first day before continuing to Poconé and the Transpantaneira.

fieldData.excerpt: A five-hour drive from Phoenix that almost didn't happen, a crowd of strangers all saying wow at the same rim, and a long climb down to the Colorado River to kayak.
fieldData.body:
As part of our shared hobby, my wife and I decided to visit Horseshoe Bend, a unique and world-famous spot. Located near the Grand Canyon, it stretches across three states: Arizona, Utah, and Colorado. Initially, I wasn't too excited. It seemed like just another tourist attraction, and it was a five-hour drive from Phoenix, Arizona. After flying to Phoenix, we debated whether the long drive through the desert would be worth it. But in the end, we decided to go for it and set off toward the Grand Canyon.

When we arrived at the park, all I could see was the desert and cacti. We followed the trail signs along with a crowd of other visitors, walking toward what looked like a stone mountain. After just a few minutes, we reached the edge and… wow! The view was breathtaking. We were standing atop Horseshoe Bend, looking down at the Colorado River winding through the canyon. I hadn't expected it to be this beautiful.

To explore further, we had to descend thousands of steps to reach the river for a kayaking adventure. It took around 30 to 40 minutes to get down, but the experience was absolutely worth the effort. Everyone around us, like us, could only say 'wow.' We paused, took it all in, and marveled at the sheer beauty of this incredible place.

fieldData.excerpt: A last-minute trip to the German border for Sort Sol, the marshland murmuration that only does the famous part when something tries to eat it. Plus the falcon that never showed, and the correct way to cross the Fyn bridge.
fieldData.body:
Here is what nobody tells you about the Black Sun: it is a bedtime.

Up to a million starlings (iridescent, loud, and far better looking than their reputation) spend the day eating their way across the marshes of southern Denmark, and then, in the twenty minutes after sunset, every one of them goes to sleep in the same patch of reeds. That is the event. That is what people drive in from many countries to see. Birds, turning in.

I am officially one of those people now. I would do it again. This is how birdwatching becomes a recurring appointment in your calendar.

I planned this one as a solo trip. My main squeeze, Jay, got in the car anyway, and the pack dog was close behind. No RSVP, just seatbelt.

Here is my actual method for finding somewhere new in a country I have already seen a lot of: I open Google Photos, stare at the heat map, and hunt for the blank spots. Denmark is small enough that the blank spots are now a competitive sport, and I am in aggressive cost-saving mode, which means the search radius is whatever I can drive before my coffee wears off. There was one blank patch left, down by the German border in Jutland. When I went looking for what was in it, I found out that in late September, the sky down there fills up.

They call it Sort Sol, the Black Sun.

What Sort Sol actually is

Starlings gather in the marshlands of southern Denmark and northern Germany on their way south, feeding in the fields all day and coming in at dusk to roost in the reeds. When enough of them arrive at once, they blot out the light. Hence the name.

The part nobody tells you until you are standing in a wet field: the famous shapes only happen when the birds are frightened. A falcon comes in, the flock tightens, and every bird starts tracking the seven or so birds nearest to it, which is enough to turn hundreds of thousands of individual animals into one object that moves like liquid and reads, to a predator, as something much too large to eat. No falcon, no shapes. Just a great deal of arriving.

We got a great deal of arriving. I am not going to pretend we got a cathedral in the sky, because we did not, and half the people standing near us were on night three of trying. The birds clocked in, did their shift, and went to bed. I will take it.

Getting there, and the windows-down thing

We crossed onto Fyn in the middle of the afternoon, and I did what I always do on that bridge: I put every window down.

Nobody taught me this. You can see the wind sail along the span, and on a real day the gusts will shove the car sideways enough that you have to hold the wheel like you mean it. So I open every window, let the wind slap me awake until my eyes water, and sing over it badly. Regular readers know there is already a Fyn bridge tradition here, involving humming "Tequila" about two dozen times on a previous crossing. This was the sequel. At this rate, that bridge is getting its own tag.

Somewhere on the drive we stopped to charge, and because a charge stop is twenty-five minutes of standing in a field pretending to look at your phone, Magnus and I sang to a herd of cows. The cows were unmoved. Magnus was delighted. I maintain this is the correct use of the time.

Just after the bridge we stopped at Café Stribo for lunch, where the owners were the loveliest people we met all weekend, and that includes the birds. Jay raved about his milkshake online, which for him is a formal review.

Finding the birds

Most guides will tell you to book a local nature guide, and you should. Tour operators run evening buses out into the marsh; they know the roosts, and these are small businesses in a very small corner of the country. We were not trying to dodge that. I was just last-minute enough that everything was full.

So I did it the other way: there is a roost map online that shows where the flocks came down the night before, and I used that, plus a lot of searching, to pick a target, which is a fine plan as long as you understand the catch. These birds short-term migrate around the wider Tønder marshlands. They don't commute to the same address every evening. They are looking for safe reeds and good feeding, and if the falcons found them last night, they will be somewhere else tonight. Yesterday's roost is a hint, not a reservation.

Driving in, we started seeing starlings on the power lines and little twisting drops into the fields, and we were thrilled, because we assumed that was the show. Reader, that was the parking lot.

We pulled in first at a little marina about a kilometer from Aventoft, set out our chairs and blankets and drinks, and felt very clever. Then the tour buses went past, in a convoy that made our cleverness look like amateur hour. We packed up and followed them. They took us to Grænsekro in Rudbøl, a cafe and restaurant sitting on the water in the marsh.

Which is exactly where I had been headed in the first place.

That is the whole lesson, honestly. Trust your research until the buses disagree with you, then follow the buses. The buses have a guide on board who has been doing this since before you knew what a starling was.

Every starling in Denmark clocks out at 6:45

By 6:15, thousands of people were on the bridges and the banks. By 6:45 there were hundreds of thousands of birds.

They come in from every angle in separate flocks, and here is the detail I was not ready for: as they beat their wings, catching the last of the light, the whole flock glitters like someone shook out a sheet of sequins over the marsh. It is the kind of sparkle you do not expect from a bird that spends its day in a ditch.

We watched them stack up, circle, and pour down into the reeds, surrounded by people from what sounded like a dozen countries, all making the same noise. I also received several unsolicited comments about the size of my telephoto lens. All of them were, I want to stress, entirely sincere. Birdwatchers are a direct people.

Dinner in another country

Aventoft is about a kilometer over the border, so we drove into Germany for dinner. Jay had schnitzel. I had salmon and a baked potato. There is something deeply satisfying about watching a marsh full of birds go to bed, crossing an international border for dinner, and being home in Copenhagen by the following evening. To be fair, that is roughly what the birds do this time of year too. Cross the border for some eats before bedtime.

Car camping, with one complication

I had booked Brændebro Camping for about 90 kroner, roughly thirteen USD, purely because I wanted somewhere I could legally car camp. It turned out to have outdoor cooking areas, bathrooms, showers, and a fitness facility across the road. That is an absurd amount of infrastructure for the price. Denmark does not mess around with campsites.

A note on this, because I do not want to oversell it: Denmark is not a park-anywhere country. What Denmark is very good at is affordable, well-run pitches, and if you are willing to pay for a spot, you will usually find a good one for a tent, a car, or an RV. The caveat is that during Sort Sol season, everything near the marshes sells out, which was my first real clue that this bird thing was a much bigger deal than I had understood. Book something.

Now the complication. This was Magnus's first car camp. The back of our Mercedes GLB 350 4MATIC sleeps one adult comfortably, two adults less comfortably, and that math does not survive adding a 35-kilo Samoyed who installs himself down the center. The upside: we barely touched the climate controls all night, because we had a living heated blanket. The downside: rolling over became a negotiation involving three parties, one of whom does not speak and none of whom were prepared to compromise.

We are upgrading the setup this week and going out again next weekend.

Sunday

We drove onto the beach at Rømø, which you can do, because it is a drive-on beach and it is enormous. We made coffee on the sand and ate pastries from a local bakery while the dog lost his mind about the horizon. There is a specific joy in drinking coffee on a beach you drove onto yourself.

Then Esbjerg, because Jay had somehow never seen Men at Sea, the four enormous white figures staring out at the water. Then home, with a stop at Apoli in Nyborg and a look at the castle and its moats.

We had meant to stop in Odense for lunch. On the drive out, Jay had asked, apropos of nothing, when the Hans Christian Andersen Marathon was and whether we should sign up. We drove into Odense on Sunday to find the city closed for the Hans Christian Andersen Marathon.

We did not get lunch. We are signing up for next year.

What I would tell you

Book a guide if you can. Book a pitch either way. Hold the location loosely, because the birds are not holding it at all. Get there by six and stay past sunset. And if you are driving over Fyn to get there, put your windows down.

Two days, one country border, one very cheap campsite, one dog who is now a permanent fixture of the bed.

fieldData.short-version: Sort Sol, the Black Sun, is a starling murmuration that happens in the marshlands of southwestern Jutland and northern Germany in spring and autumn, as up to a million birds gather at dusk to roost in the reeds. The famous liquid shapes only form when a predator such as a falcon attacks and the flock tightens, with each bird tracking roughly its seven nearest neighbors, so a still evening means arrival without spectacle. The flocks move around the wider Tønder marshlands night to night, so last night's roost is not a guarantee. Local operators run evening bus tours from the area and are the most reliable way to find the birds. We drove down from Copenhagen for a weekend in late September 2026, watched from Grænsekro in Rudbøl, and car camped nearby for about 90 kroner.
fieldData.quick-answers:
What is Sort Sol?

Sort Sol, or the Black Sun, is the name for the huge starling murmurations that gather over the marshlands of southwestern Jutland at dusk, when enough birds arrive at once to darken the sky before they drop into the reeds to roost.

When can you see the Black Sun in Denmark?

Spring and autumn, while the starlings are migrating between southern Europe and Scandinavia. We went in late September. It happens in the hour or so after sunset.

Where do you see it?

The marshlands of southwestern Jutland, especially around Tønder and Ribe, and across the border into northern Germany. We watched from Grænsekro in Rudbøl, right on the Danish-German border.

Why don't you always see the famous shapes?

The shapes are a defense. When a falcon or other predator attacks, the flock tightens and each bird tracks roughly the seven birds nearest to it, which turns the group into one large shifting object. On a night with no predator, you get the arrival and the roosting but not the sculpture.

Do you need a guide?

You do not strictly need one, but local operators run evening buses, know the current roosts, and are small businesses worth supporting. Book ahead, because they fill up in season.

Will the birds be in the same place two nights running?

Not reliably. They short-term migrate around the wider marshland looking for safe reeds and good feeding, so a roost map tells you where they were last night, not where they will be tonight.

What does it cost?

Very little if you drive and camp. Our campsite was about 90 kroner, roughly 13 US dollars. Guided bus tours and accommodation in the area cost more and sell out during the season.

Can you car camp in Denmark?

Not anywhere you like. Denmark is not a park-anywhere country, but it has plenty of affordable, well-run campsites that take tents, cars and RVs. In Sort Sol season the ones near the marshes sell out, so book something.

fieldData.excerpt: When you are seeking that spark of life, you chase it. Carnaval in Salvador with 2.5 million people, a desert that fills with water every year, and six days on the Rio Negro with pink dolphins and one sloth with somewhere to be.
fieldData.body:
When you are seeking that spark of life, you chase it. In our case, we followed a drumline north until the road ran out and the Amazon started.

Nobody tells you that awe is renewable, but you can still run out. We were living in São Paulo, a city I love enough to forgive its traffic, and I had reached the point where I could walk past a samba parade or a tree full of marsupials on my way to buy dish soap. The passport was getting stamps. The personal inspiration was not.

So we went north. No international flights, no visa runs, not even a single chat with an immigration officer about my handwriting. Just Brazil, doing what Brazil does best: reminding you to look up.

Salvador: the math does not work, and it happens anyway

Salvador, Bahia, is less a city than an exclamation mark with an airport.

Carnaval here is not a festival. A festival has a perimeter. This has roughly 2.5 million people in it, about 1.5 million of them visitors, moving through the streets behind trucks the size of buildings. The camarotes (the elevated boxes you buy your way into, which is the civilized way to do this) put you above the crowd with a drink in your hand and a view of a human river that does not stop for six days.

The soundtrack was Léo Santana, Ivete Sangalo, Alok, and at one point, for reasons I have never been able to reconstruct, the Squid Game theme over fireworks on the beach. It worked. Everything works there. The normal rules about what goes with what are suspended for the week.

If you go, book your camarote tickets early. We used Carnaval.com, which worked, but the real trick is deciding what you are willing to lose before you even leave the hotel. Not a burner phone for the story, but a real, honest inventory of what you can watch disappear into a crowd of two million. The energy is contagious. So is the pickpocketing. Both are running at Olympic level.

Lençóis Maranhenses: the desert that fills up

After six days of that, we needed the opposite of Salvador, and Brazil keeps one.

Lençóis Maranhenses is a few hundred square miles of white dunes that look exactly like a desert and behave like nothing of the kind. Wind carries sand inland off the coast and piles it into ridges. Underneath it all sits rock that water cannot get through. So when the rains come, and about seventy percent of the year's rain falls between January and May, the water cannot drain anywhere. It just collects in the valleys between the dunes.

What you get, a few months later, is a desert with thousands of freshwater lagoons in it. Blue, warm, clear enough to see your own feet. Then the dry season arrives, and the whole thing evaporates at up to a meter a month until it is a desert again, and the following January it starts over.

We swam, floated, and walked barefoot over ridgelines under a sky so wide it seemed to absorb sound. The sand squeaks underfoot. That is the detail I still think about.

If you go: fly into São Luís (SLZ) and get yourself to Barreirinhas with someone who knows the roads. Timing is everything. June and July are when the lagoons are full and the sand is still cool enough to walk on. By August, some of the pools are already shrinking, and by September, most of them have called it a year. Atins dries up first, Santo Amaro holds out the longest. If anyone tries to sell you a September lagoon trip, ask to see their definition of "full."

Anavilhanas: six days of the jungle not caring about your inbox

Then the grand finale: six days at Anavilhanas Jungle Lodge, on the Rio Negro, deep enough in that the concept of a notification stops applying.

The Rio Negro does not flow so much as linger. The jungle does not whisper. It runs at volume, in every direction, all night, and then hands you a completely different set of sounds at dawn. Time behaves strangely out there. Six days felt like two weeks in the best possible way.

We swam with pink and gray dolphins. We napped in hammocks. We chased rainstorms across the water. We listened for tapirs every single day and never saw one, which I have made peace with.

And we watched a sloth swim across the river, doing the world's most committed slow crawl with somewhere clearly to be. I have never in my life wanted to hand an animal a pool noodle so badly. I didn't, because you don't, but the urge was overwhelming, and Jay can confirm I talked about it for two days.

The food deserves its own paragraph. Fish steamed in banana leaves. A menu full of things that sound like incantations (jambu, cupuaçu, bacaba). Caipirinhas on the dock made with limes from somewhere within walking distance. I have eaten at restaurants with three times the pedigree and half the memorability.

Wildlife roll call: red macaws, boa constrictors, iguanas, caimans, howler monkeys, tarantulas, and one Goliath bird-eating spider who has been living rent-free in my brain ever since. I would like it to leave.

Magnus Waffles stayed home for this one. We missed him with every monkey screech, which is saying something, because there were a lot of monkey screeches.

What I would tell you

Do them in this order. Salvador first, while you still have the stamina, then the dunes, then the river. Going the other way would be a crime against your nervous system.

Leave yourself more time than you think between Salvador and anywhere that expects you to use your inside voice. Carnaval does not let you walk away at a normal human pace. I tried. My ears are still ringing.

And the bigger thing, which is the actual reason this trip worked: I did not have to leave the country to be astonished. I had to leave the part of the country I had gotten used to. Awe is not a place. It is a state of mind, and mine had gotten lazy. Brazil fixed that in about nine hours flat, starting with a drumline.

From Carnaval's chaos to dune silence to a river that hums, this one gave Jay and me back something we had misplaced: each other, our curiosity, and a pink dolphin or two.

We did this trip from São Paulo, where we were living at the time, with no international flights involved.
fieldData.quick-answers:
How many people go to Carnaval in Salvador?

Roughly 2.5 million, about 1.5 million of them visitors. It runs for six days through the streets of the city, following trucks carrying the bands.

What is a camarote?

An elevated private box you buy a ticket for, raised above the street crowd, usually with drinks included. It is the comfortable way to experience Carnaval in Salvador. Book well in advance.

Is Carnaval in Salvador safe?

Pickpocketing is common and organized. The practical approach is not a burner phone as a gimmick but an honest decision about what you are willing to lose before you go out, and taking nothing else into the crowd.

Why does Lençóis Maranhenses fill with water?

Wind blows coastal sand inland into dunes that sit on rock water cannot pass through. About 70 percent of the annual rain falls between January and May, and with nowhere to drain, it collects in the valleys between the dunes as thousands of freshwater lagoons.

When are the Lençóis Maranhenses lagoons full?

June and July are the peak. By August some pools are shrinking, and by September most are gone. In the dry season the water evaporates at up to a meter a month. Atins dries out first and Santo Amaro holds water the longest.

How do you get to Lençóis Maranhenses?

Fly into São Luís (SLZ) and travel on to Barreirinhas, which is the usual base for the dunes. Go with a guide who knows the roads.

Where is Anavilhanas Jungle Lodge?

On the Rio Negro in the Brazilian Amazon, near the Anavilhanas archipelago. We stayed six days.

Can you see pink dolphins on the Rio Negro?

Yes. Both pink and gray river dolphins live in the Rio Negro and we swam with them. Tapirs are much harder; we listened every day and never saw one.

What order should you do these three places in?

Salvador first, while you still have the energy, then the dunes, then the river. Leave more time than you think between Carnaval and anywhere quiet.

fieldData.excerpt: A friend's wedding outside Madrid, free tapas with every drink, a Keinemusik night at La Caja Mágica, then a villa in Ibiza and a ferry to Formentera.
fieldData.body:
Arriving in Madrid, Spain felt like pure bliss. The air was fresh, and the sunny day was filled with light as we prepared to explore the city's hidden gems before our friend's wedding on Sunday.

We stayed at Hotel De Toledo, centrally located and perfect for walking around and discovering the area. Our first stop was for patatas bravas at a local spot where, with each drink, you get a free tapa, no questions asked, no chairs, just standing around, drinking, and chatting with friends. Perfecto!

We wandered through alleyways and quaint shops before a quick gelato stop on our way to Siroco, a techno club on the northwest side of town, where my boyfriend had a show. The club has two rooms with different vibes, so if you're looking for something unique in Madrid's nightlife, it's a must-visit.

After a late night, we spent the next day hopping from café to restaurant to bar (Sahurao Madrid and Ok Hostel are great spots). We met a wonderful woman from the Balearic Islands, who mentioned a Keinemusik show at La Caja Mágica that evening. It was perfect, since we're big fans. We joined her and danced the night away.

The sunset that evening was a watercolor painting of fiery hues, setting the stage for an unforgettable night of dancing, singing, and enjoying great company, both old and new. In Spain, everyone is friendly, and life feels more relaxed. All you need is a drink, tapas, good music, and great company.

Madrid's architecture also takes you back in time, with its rich history still very much alive in the city streets.

The wedding

Sunday was the big day, time for the wedding. We took a bus to Fábricas De Harinas, a hacienda just outside the city, straight out of a fairytale. The Indian-Spanish ceremony was beautiful, with translations in Hindi, Spanish, and English, as the bride grew up in Canada. The night was filled with laughter, tears, sparkling wine, a delicious courtyard dinner, dancing, and lots of music. We fell asleep with warm, fuzzy feelings from a joyous celebration of love.

Ibiza

The next day, we headed to Spain's famous island, Ibiza. Having been there before with a local friend, this time was different: we were staying in a villa with the wedding party. The villa, located on the quieter northeast side of the island, offered a peaceful retreat, though still close enough to join in the party atmosphere when desired.

Ibiza is special because you can strike a balance between lively nightlife and peaceful relaxation. The island's beauty is palpable, and the energy is ever-present.

Our first evening was spent at Playa Soleil for the All Day I Dream party, enjoying amazing sushi and Greek salad. The second night, we dined at S'Illa Des Bosc with the wedding party and tried Ibiza's famous black rice paella. With the restaurant perched on cliffs and the sunset painting the sky, it was a perfect evening.

The following night, we partied with Fisher at Hï Ibiza. If you're going to one of these big clubs, I'd recommend the VIP option, especially if you don't arrive early. The crowds can be intense, and visibility can be an issue! But the energy was high, and we danced until morning.

Formentera

The next day, we took a ferry to Formentera, a stunning island just 40 minutes from Ibiza Town. The island narrows during high tide, creating a thin strip of beach with ocean views on both sides. It's a breathtaking sight. The ferry drops you off at the dock, where a bus takes you to the beach. The last bus returns to the ferry around 6 p.m.

Spain is absolutely stunning, with friendly people, incredible food, laid-back vibes, and countless beautiful places to explore.

fieldData.excerpt: As one does, my friends arrived, so I took them to a Danish bog. Three countries, one opinionated Samoyed, a lot of pastries, and a trip bookended by the North Sea and the Baltic.
fieldData.body:
🇩🇰🇸🇪🇳🇴

As one does, my friends arrived, so I took them to a Danish bog.

We walked the bog, dripping with rain and looking for birds. They finished the trip dipping in the sea. Needless to say, we were wet.

In between: three countries, one opinionated Samoyed, and more chai lattes than I'll ever admit to ordering.

For context: I live in Copenhagen, where we have pastries, canals, and supermodels on bikes. Rye bread works wonders for the abs. What I don't always have is someone to see it fresh with.

Enter Melinda: bestie since Pogs and Winnie the Pooh sweatshirts. The kind of friend you have matching bracelets and embarrassing dance videos with, and can pick up with after years apart as if nothing happened. She landed with her daughter Jaden, who was finally celebrating her graduation from a few years back. Jaden is a wildlife person. Birds, especially. Her favorite is the pigeon. Not a typo. She does not rank the world the way the rest of us do. The trip was better for it.

The perfect amount of lag. This is Scandinavia through their eyes.

Denmark via Møns: 497 steps and a sled dog with momentum

We started local: a marshy bog near Magnus's frisør. Yes, my dog has a hairdresser, Denmark things. There was open access to stinky sheep. A swan nearly attacked me while protecting her cygnets. It rained, but it was still beautiful. That's the Danish deal.

Then Møns Klint. Led by Hart Bageri. That sugar-topped cardamom bun is famous for a reason. We hit a different pastry shop most days.

Magnus Waffles, my Samoyed, came along. This mattered on the stairs. The Maglevand staircase is 497 steps. Magnus is a sled dog. Being pulled down 497 steps by an animal bred to pull is a quad workout no gym can match. Worth the hobbling for days: white chalk cliffs, wildlife, good friends at the bottom. And a doggy poo moment. Only 497 steps to carry dog poo up.

Hit the chai latte. September in the Nordics, you need something warm in your hands. That is the hygge entry fee.

The girls tried smørrebrød. Not their favorite. The pastrami version ran salty. My usuals, curried herring and plaice, were missing from the menu. Next time. They ate it anyway. That counts as integrating.

We drove past a viking celebration. They are as common here as farmers' markets are back home. Rainy boardwalks. Thatched roofs. We climbed the forest tower at Camp Adventure for a quick pocket of sunshine. Wind turbines in the distance. Local Danes climbing past, polishing off their Tuborgs. Between here and Dyrehaven: plenty of elk. Deer, technically, but Jaden and I stand by our ID. Goats too.

Back in Copenhagen, we biked to Gasoline Grill on the canals. Not every American grew up on a bicycle, but every Dane did. The post Jaden nearly ran into noticed too. She was equally graceful (or not) on the metro.

We took in an evening at Dyrehaven and Bakken.

For race day: Melinda and I took on the Ørestad 10K, an absurdly beautiful morning by the sea. Jay ran the half. Jaden walked with Magnus. We saw ponies. Kids with Danish flags ran by laughing and dancing. We chose Union Kitchen for brunch, my most trusted breakfast decision in this city.

Klampenborg for a walk. More chai. Roskilde for the Viking Ship Museum and the Rockmuseet. I preferred it being called Ragnarock.

Helsingør: hunting sea amber. Years here and I only just learned. Kids with nets on stormy days are not chasing jellyfish. They are after amber. The internet says: drop your find in salt water. Amber floats. Ours sank. Every piece. Still fun. And the girls casually took in a castle because Europe.

Sweden, or: a moose safari and the world's biggest cinnamon bun

Then the road trip. Me, Melinda, Jaden. We assigned everyone a color to photograph. Claude picked. I got yellow. Sounds like a game for children. It is the fastest way to make three adults notice a country. My camera roll: wildflowers, bees, butterflies, apples, Swedish flag. Corners of southern Sweden. Then the moose safari. The moose came close enough for genuinely great photos. The resident American bison looked, in my professional opinion, jet-lagged from the move to Europe. Been there, friends.

We slept in cute cabins on an apple orchard. Woke to slugs in morning fog over a small lake, more adorable than it sounds. The girls had Swedish meatballs; I had smoked salmon salad and rösti. In Gothenburg, Jaden got her pigeons, so many pigeons! The girls got licorice (I abstained from far away). A puppy nibbled my finger. First cinnamon buns of the trip: world's biggest, at the famous shop in Haga. Go big or go home. We hunted for wooden Dala horses. Jaden chased small birds, semi-professionally.

Norway, or: moss roofs and a lake serpent

After a quick ferry hop past a Gothic church, we were in Norway, where the roofs stop being thatched and start growing moss, a national upgrade I fully endorse. A rest stop introduced us to the Seljord lake serpent, which famously controls its lake and controlled our sense of humor for the rest of the drive.

Our next cabin was called Eldhuset. We woke to sunrise. Locals winter-dipping in glacier lakes on the plateau. Casual. We fed more sheep. Passed famous waterfalls on the road to Odda and Thor's Hammer land. Another chai latte. More sweets. Plums straight from an orchard. Drove through fjord country with our faces against the windows.

Bergen. We took the funicular up. Hiked down through the troll rainforest. Cuddly sheep. Like they actually liked to be touched. Tourists with the same good idea. Sushi for dinner. Norway introduced salmon to sushi. Eating it here is visiting the source. Next morning: sunrise walk with Melinda. After breakfast, I ran to the bridge to stand under something that big.

Last big hike: Kjeldebu. Under the glacier on the Hardanger plateau. Prettiest autumn colors I have ever seen. Night in a DNT cabin. Prescribing it to everyone. Then the drive to Kristiansand. Ferry to Hirtshals.

The bookend

Last countryside night. Danish coast at Skallerup. Walked into the North Sea for a proper sea bath. Although proper was not the right word, seeing as the ramp was partially missing in the sea, the dip was more of a tuck and let giant waves splash over the top of you. One more meal together. Woke to Icelandic ponies and burros on the farm. Back home: femkamp at Tivoli with Jay.

Final morning. Melinda, Jay, and I dipped in the Baltic. Canals outside our home. Melinda bookended her trip in two seas. North Sea and Baltic. Top and tail of Scandinavia. Everything above squeezed in between. Three countries. One color game. One supervising Samoyed. The kind of camaraderie that makes even a rainy bog feel like the point. Hole-in-the-wall pastry (a new fav) at Kong Hans before the airport run, and you guessed it, one final chai before departure.

The debrief

Personal moments · What was your favorite moment with Melinda and Jaden?
Group consensus: hiking to the DNT cabin. Nature meets comfort meets adventure. Highly recommend. Get your DNT key.

Inside jokes · Any funny stories or mishaps you left out?
Two. One: we hiked to Denmark's tallest peak, Møllehøj, faked pain and challenge with every step, then celebrated entirely too big at the top. Two: humming "Tequila" on the Fyn bridge, windows wide open. We did it over two dozen times. Super freeing. (It is a one-word song. Everyone can join.)

Samoyed details · Magnus's most dramatic moment?
The Møns Klint poo felt like comeuppance.

Food adventures · The group's favorite?
We loved the food tour enough to repeat it: a return trip to Gasoline Grill, and unanimous love for Juno and the hole-in-the-wall pastries at Kong Hans.

Travel tips · Would you recommend these spots for a family trip?
Definitely, with one rule: break up your Scandinavian trip and see more than just the cities. The bogs, orchards, and plateaus are where this one actually happened.

hero-image.alt: La Paz, Baja California Sur, Mexico

fieldData.excerpt: Wider than your sense of scale, moving with an ease that is almost funny once the initial shock wears off. Then the sea lions, who chose chaos.
fieldData.body:
Crossed across the pond, detoured through LA, and in a move that feels aggressively on-brand, went from Latin America to Europe and straight back to Mexico. Slightly glamorous chaos. Enter: La Paz.

Mornings were for marina runs and early starts. The rest unfolded exactly as it should. Tacos when it mattered. I was reunited with my sisters for the first time in ages. The jazzy one. The tall one. And my dad and Kimie, fully game for adventure, early departures, and saying yes to whatever came next.

Day one came with roadside wild horses, setting the tone just casually.

The ocean reminded us who is actually in charge

WHALE SHARKS. Huge. Polka-dotted. Gentle giants. Silently drifting past, wider than your sense of scale, moving with an ease that is almost funny once the initial holy sh*t wears off. Majestic. Calm.

Meanwhile, I am absolutely more like a sea lion when it comes to aquatic life.

Sea lions, true to form, chose chaos. One bold little menace grabbed scuba fins and played tug-of-war with our instructor's safety rope. No fear. Full confidence.

Many of our tours were led by marine biology students and researchers, which made the experience even better. Not just beautiful, but informed. Protected waters, real conservation, and people who genuinely care for this underwater world. If you want to do the same, look for operators who prioritize responsible practices: choose tours that follow local regulations, allow only small groups, and have guides who are knowledgeable about conservation. Bonus points if the company works with scientists or supports habitat protection. Asking questions about their environmental policies can help you make sure your visit is actually helping, not harming, the place you're there to enjoy.

Between it all: sea lion swims, pelicans everywhere, beachside ceviche, top-shelf margaritas, garden-fresh Brussels sprouts that had no business being that good, and a very necessary Costco run because it is bulking season.

Road trips, sunrise hikes, and Hotel California

Jess and I road-tripped all o'er. One drive up a hill through a construction zone to our rental. Another trip to Cabo for pastries and landscaping views worthy of a moment of their own.

A sunrise hike with Dad and Kimie came with sweeping views of Playa Balandra, a moonrise glistening across the sea, and street puppies with suspiciously wholesome attitudes. Todos Santos wrapped it up with quiet beachside nights, stars overhead, and a stop at Hotel California because obviously.

On the return LA stopover, I landed exactly where I needed to. Cafe Gratitude with Jo and Scott, plus Jenn, reading affirmations like "I am goofy," "I am lovely," and "I am a runner." And, honestly, yes to all three.

And because I live abroad and travel like an immigrant on a mission, there was also the LA unboxing ritual. Cold meds. So many cold meds.

I miss my family deeply, especially around the holidays. But this kind of time together, this kind of choosing adventure and connection? I would say yes again and again.

fieldData.excerpt: Some people do vision boards. We did blisters. An accelerated W Trek over Christmas, a rainbow nobody deserved, and a New Year in the golden light at Estancia Bonanza.
fieldData.body:
How we kicked off the new year with wind, wine, and enjoyably questionable decisions

Some people do vision boards. We did blisters.

This adventure started with a flight route that raised several eyebrows and at least one TSA sigh:

Copenhagen to Helsinki to Miami to Punta Cana to Santiago.

Questionable. Ambitious. Deeply on brand.

The first layover kicked off with a cold plunge. Not the cute kind.

At Löylykontti (Helsinki) at midnight in December, we sprinted straight from the sauna into the Baltic Sea, which was thrashing the rocks like it had personal beef with us. Violent. Loud. Absolutely not for the weak. There is no photo evidence because "Finnish sauna" is sacred, under-clothed, and phones are felt to be disrespectful.

The Miami layover involved evening drinks at the marina, because staying at airports is for the sane.

Punta Cana was too short to leave the airport, foiling yet again the attempt to visit the DR, but we are certain our flight to Santiago appreciated our Taco Bell dinner.

Reunions, runners, luchador masks

Breakfast in Santiago reunited us first with Drew and Allen, two of our beloved Pacific Northwesterners, who arrived donning luchador masks and motivational attitudes. Our Fellow Runners with Kickball origin stories. Allen goes by Danger. Drew loves horses. Two couples are freshly separated from their very loved dogs. Their doodle, Leo, at the family holiday fest in Portland. Our Sami, Sir Magnus Waffles, is holding down the fort and writing his biopic with our extended family, the Meadows, back in Denmark. The adventure hit a little harder because of it.

Dinner and drinks with some of our favorites, Mati and Ainura, followed. City tour. Ceviche. Pisco sours. Pool time. A life-size gingerbread house that had no business being there but somehow worked. Santiago was the soft landing before heading south.

Logistics season begins

An early flight dropped us in Punta Arenas, where logistics officially took over. Then it was a puzzle to store the luggage (Jay paid a guy to borrow his car), catch the boat, and make it to Magdalena Island. Itty bitty penguins everywhere. Elephant seals. Wind is doing what wind does best in Patagonia, asserting dominance. Warm cocoa on deck.

Back in town, our check-in guy showed up wearing a Bend, Oregon Blockbuster shirt. The universe remains extremely committed to the bit. Gear checks. Butane. Pickles. Charcuterie. The things you never want to realize you forgot once you're already committed.

Christmas Eve, but make it brisket

Christmas Eve brought another cozy bus and our arrival in Puerto Natales. Expecting closed shops, we instead rented missing gear, found brisket, and somehow secured a table at Last Hope Distillery. Calafate Gin. Cervejas. A moose-like dessert that looked suspiciously like Torres del Paine.

Christmas Day, parrot shirts, and pickle diplomacy

On Christmas Day, we donned our FARM Rio parrot shirts and officially hit the trail. Bus. Breezy catamaran. Unreal views of Torres del Paine National Park. Lunch featured Allen's pickles (which, unfortunately, he didn't get any of) and camp sandwiches. Peak-season campsite availability dictated the plan, so we leaned into an accelerated W Trek. Windy hills. Guanacos on the transfer. Views that did not feel real.

Night one at Camp Francés included repeated walk-bys of Camp Italiano, now a formal unit of measurement. We decorated a Christmas tree with pinecones, cinnamon sticks, and dried oranges. Discovered the camp bar. Drank a little too much Chilean red wine. Allen performed unintentional gymnastics off his tent ladder while wearing a luchador mask (as one does) and survived. Another ladder claimed a second victim later (let's be real, it was Nancy). New friends. Christmas, Patagonia style.

Boxing Day: character building, apparently

Boxing Day was a push. Oatmeal breakfast. Thirty-three kilometers. Mirador Británico delivered a horizon-wide rainbow that felt wildly undeserved and absolutely perfect. Camp Italiano appeared again. And again. Waterfalls roaring. Wind tunnels on pebble beaches. Calves filing formal complaints.

A surprise puma sighting at camp boosted morale, but we missed him. Horses grazed casually as we walked into Central Camp, like this was all very normal. Empanadas. Camp meals. Immediate sleep.

The Towers, the wind, and choosing smart

Day six came fast. Drew and I navigated to the Towers at 4:00 a.m. Short sleep. Big wind. Ninety percent chance of rain. Gusts strong enough to remind us that not quitting and making smart safety calls are, in fact, different skill sets. We turned back on the ridge due to visibility and conditions, as recommended locally.

Later, we returned our very stinky gear, celebrated properly back at our ol' friend El Brisket, and quietly held space on the trail. Jay was already thinking about where the next craft beer might be.

Borders, beers, and too many fries

Another sleeper bus carried us across the border into Argentina, complete with stray dogs who appeared to be enforcing customs. El Calafate delivered immediately. Craft brews. Burgers at La Zorro. Beers at Patagonia Brewing. On our first night, we accidentally ordered five portions of French fries. Language barriers are real. We ate them all. The post-hike crew rose to the occasion.

Ice, condors, and a proper tradition

The glaciers at Los Glaciares National Park were next. Another bus, whoo-hoo. A perfect sunny day on the water. Bright blue ice towering over boats. A condor perched on a rock face, immediately named Diego by the kids onboard.

Before leaving Perito Moreno Glacier, we revived a long-standing tradition. Whiskey on glacier rocks. Cold air. Blue ice. Perspective served neat. Some "neat" traditions.

Miles, mate, and a proper send-off

Our final day in El Calafate was spent walking intentionally to reach 1,000 miles for the year. Mate shopping. Gaucho poncho hunting. Flamingos at Laguna Nimez. A decadent celebratory dinner at MAKO with oysters, parrilla, and a paired local vinho menu.

A later start finally brought us to El Chaltén. Afternoon hike to Mirador de los Cóndores. No bird sightings, but flawless visibility. Nordic-inspired tiny homes felt exactly right.

New Year's Eve, but with horses

New Year's Eve took us into the countryside. More gaucho shopping. Horseback riding through the hills. Farm dogs chasing rabbits. One dog ran the entire route like a horse and should be promoted accordingly. A brand-new kitten. Dinner at Estancia Bonanza with Fitz Roy watching quietly as the sun dipped low. We danced in the golden light, drank Argentine wine, ate like barbecue kings, tango'd to live music, and welcomed the new year by the iconic view.

New year, same legs

New Year's Day came with snoozed alarms and a later 10:00am trail start. Drew, Jay, and I hiked with Allen in our thoughts every blistered step. Strong legs. Slower pace. Sandwiches bigger than your head. Ten kilometers later, plus two Multnomah Falls' worth of elevation, we drank icy water from the Río Blanco, watched condors glide overhead, and soaked in watercolor views of Fitz Roy, helicopter rescues, and the surrounding lakes. In town, Allen closed out a rough year in the most perfect of venues. Dinner with the full crew sealed it.

On our final day, we bused back to El Calafate and flew to Santiago, hoping to squeeze in one last night outing before heading our separate ways.

Patagonia felt like a reset. A send-off. A slightly unhinged but very intentional way to step into the new year. We arrived counting kilometers and left counting everything in Camp Italianos.

And yes, the whole thing was worth it. Even the flight route. Even the Taco Bell.

fieldData.quick-answers:
How long is the W Trek?

We ran an accelerated version because peak-season campsite availability dictated it (six months out, and a campsite broker was involved). Boxing Day alone was thirty-three kilometers. My legs still remember.

Can you hike Torres del Paine at Christmas?

Yes, and the campsites fill up. We decorated a tree with pinecones, cinnamon sticks, and dried oranges at Camp Frances. Patagonia Christmas, achieved.

Should you push for the Towers in bad weather?

We did not. Ninety percent chance of rain and gusts on the ridge, so we turned back on local advice. Not quitting and making smart safety calls are different skill sets. I am learning.
