fieldData.excerpt: Montenegro's roads are about to get a quiet word from Nepal, Austria and Croatia. Narrow, one-way as a suggestion, with semi-trucks reversing down mountains.
fieldData.body:
This was not a vacation. It was a work trip, and we descended on Budva in two waves.

I drove the first group out of Podgorica in a Skoda, and I would like to formally announce that Montenegro's roads are about to get a quiet word from Nepal, Austria, and Croatia. Narrow, one-way (sometimes a suggestion), overgrown, with semi-trucks reversing down mountains with the casual confidence of someone parallel-parking a Fiat.

The best drive of the week was hip-hop on blast, windows open, the road to Kotor with three colleagues, the four of us forming what I can only describe as the non-Danes club, bonded by personal histories that, at no point, involve rye bread.

Someone else had the wilder assignment. He drove a 50,000-passenger van (it was big) up a hairpin road so aggressive that even a seasoned road warrior admitted his palms were sweating. I was in that van and have never been more grateful I wasn't the one steering.

One colleague price-checked every souvenir stand in the country with Olympic-level negotiator energy. Another walked 40 kilometers into the countryside, unprompted, for funsies. He came back. We did not ask questions.

The food deserves its own paragraph.

We ate fresh fish in Budva, where our server, fully unprompted, instructed me to follow a Ukrainian lingerie Instagram account on behalf of my dog, Magnus Waffles. Magnus had no notes. The account, frankly, was committed.

Farm Carević delivered Mangalitsa fillet to our carnivores, fresh fish for the pescatarian (me), and chicken for the one chicken-iterian among us.

There was also a kneading-dough video that we watched on loop because the dough looked, unmistakably, like boobs. Boob bread. We laughed until we cried. Then we watched it again.

We stocked the house with Danish essentials (bread, cheese, Tuborg) and Nikšićko, the Balkan beer, gone too fast.

Protein was a personality trait this week. Eggs. Tuna. More eggs. Another run to the store for, you guessed it, more eggs. Engineers apparently run on protein, and I have made peace with this. So have my protein goals.

The most diverse table in Denmark

We also worked. The hard conversations happened across dinner tables and switchback drives, which is where most hard conversations belong.

Quick personal aside. We joke that we are the most diverse table in Denmark: more women than men, people from everywhere. As the token American on a properly international group, you learn fast that we are culturally loud and everyone always knows where you are. My heart is also partially Brazilian, which meant mini samba breaks throughout the week, and someone was always willing to join.

I built the team a custom welcome-drinks app using AI, because of course I did. Pomegranates, figs, and peach juice featured. Local wine featured more. Laughing featured most.
fieldData.sign-off: Sun-kissed and slightly more culturally knowledgeable than I was a week ago. Hvala Montenegro!

Narrow. One-way is more of a suggestion. Overgrown. Semi-trucks reverse down mountains with the casual confidence of someone parallel-parking a Fiat. Montenegro, you win.

Is the road to Kotor worth it?

Best drive of the week. Hip-hop on blast. Windows open. Road to Kotor, three colleagues, zero rye bread.

Fresh fish in Budva. Farm Carevic for Mangalitsa fillet, fish, and chicken all at once. No one left hungry.

fieldData.excerpt: Denmark had just thrown the coldest winter in 16 years at us, the map had a gap, and we had a few days. Then we landed in a country where everyone was wearing white except us.
fieldData.body:
People kept asking us why we trekked to Ghana (pardon the delayed post), and the honest answer is that Denmark had just thrown the coldest winter in 16 years at us, the map had a gap, and we had a few days. Sophisticated travel planning, truly.

For context on the cold, we spent weeks knocking thick ice off the canal with our Crocs (thank you, Freed, for demanding we own them) just to go winter bathing. For the uninitiated, that's the Nordic tradition of plunging into icy water, sometimes after a sauna, for the thrill and the chill-induced endorphins. -18.8°C on the worst day. Ghana sounded reasonable.

A quick layover in Amsterdam included a brief debate about whether tulips counted as a travel necessity. Verdict still pending.

We touched down in Accra dressed for a colorful print country, only to discover that in Ghana, on Easter, everyone wears all white. The whole country. Parades, brunch tables, church steps, everyone looking suspiciously photogenic. We looked like the only two people who didn't get the memo, because we were. Cue the markets, then the mall, then a slow-motion negotiation with kind strangers about where one buys white clothing in a country that, on every other day of the year, is not particularly into it.

Sorted. Mostly.

Easter brunch arrived to a soundtrack of 1990s saxophone covers and a dessert table with more Easter-themed sweets and eggs shaped as bunnies than seemed mathematically possible. Pastel everything.

We hiked Mount Afadjato, which was steeper than the brochure implied. Jay carried my water (because husbands). The view at the top was earned, but the best part was at the base, where a circle of kids drumming and singing for Easter sent the sound bouncing through the valley like the mountain had agreed to be an acoustic.

We drove on to Wli Waterfalls, then to Tafi Atome, where monkeys jumped onto our arms like it was their scheduled shift.

Back at our lodge, I made friends with Sofie, a Spanish toddler, maybe two years old, whose Spanish was roughly at my level. We had a meaningful exchange. Her parents, residents of Accra on holiday, gave us the best tip of the trip: a restaurant in town called Buka.

At Buka, I ordered veggie curry, banku, fufu, hibiscus juice, and a fresh coconut. The spice was hot, even for Jay. Three feet away, completely casually, sat the casting director for Lion King kids in London, talking about the theater in Accra.

Magnus Waffles, for the record, stayed home with our extended family, the Meadows, dressed as the Easter Bunny. I have not recovered from the photos.

Ghana gave us drumbeats, hibiscus, monkeys with no concept of personal space, and a sun warm enough to undo a Danish winter.
fieldData.sign-off: Sunburned, well-fed, slightly hibiscus-stained, Nancy and Jay

What do people wear at Easter in Ghana?

White. The whole country. Parades, brunch tables, church steps. If you show up in prints, you will be shopping for white clothes in a country that, every other day, is not particularly into them. Ask me how I know.

Is Mount Afadjato a hard hike?

Steeper than the brochure implied. The best part is at the base, where kids drum and sing and the valley bounces the sound around like it is auditioning for a music festival.

Where should you eat in Accra?

Buka. Veggie curry, banku, fufu, hibiscus juice, and a fresh coconut. The tip came from a Spanish family at our lodge who knew what was up.

fieldData.excerpt: Copenhagen to Kosovo and back in an EV, with one Samoyed operating in an advisory capacity and a back seat that ended up looking like a small artisan jam factory in transit.
fieldData.body:
As I write, my phone sits beside its charger at half battery. The charger is plugged in. The phone is not. I had ABSOLUTELY NO business driving an EV across Eastern Europe.

I did it anyway.

Copenhagen to Kosovo and back. One Samoyed operating in an advisory capacity. A back seat that, by the end, looked like a small artisan jam factory in transit. I worked remotely from Balkan lounges, a Serbian side street, and one bus that has not moved since 1974.

Apparently, when adventure relies on a charged battery, I become someone who plans. New personality trait unlocked.

Night one: a shed, as one does

We slept in a shed. In Saxony. On purpose. Magnus conducted a perimeter check, approved the premises, and went to bed after a long first day's drive, field runs, and ferry.

Czech Republic and Poland, in passing

Been there, done that, blinked across both borders. Turbines were spotted. Waved our passports at the unmanned border stops. Thanks, EU.

Slovakia, round one: Vila Kamila and the High Tatras

Tatranská Štrba. The beautiful High Tatras and glacial lakes rise out of the windshield. Vila Kamila is waiting at the end. This was the day I learned what it means to drive an EV up an actual mountain. Range goes down. The math gets dramatic. The car politely asks you to consider your decisions. Štrbské Pleso with Magnus made it worth every nervous glance at the battery icon. Recharge philosophy, established here: charge more, charge earlier, do not be brave. Or so she said.

Serbia, and the unlisted hotel charger

Belgrade welcomed us with the valet forgetting to turn off the car, followed by a non-functioning roadside charger at 11 kilometers to go, leaving us empty. Yeah, adventure, eeek! A Serbian guy noticed my Danish plate and gestured for me to follow. We did not share a language, but we shared understanding. I followed his car through a few streets, around a corner, into a hotel parking lot, where an unlisted charger for a few €s quietly waited. He pointed, nodded, and left. Western Europe, take notes, this is hospitality.

North Macedonia, the border

Belgrade to Ohrid was the plan. North Macedonia had other ideas. The border delayed me for paperwork I didn't know I needed, and yet somehow already had.

By day's end, I rerouted to Skopje and checked into a Marriott. The trip shifted here.

In Skopje, I discovered rose hip jam and ajvar over breakfast with new friends. The kind of discoveries that reorganize your pantry. It is now in the back seat. It is now in my future. It is, for the record, now a personality.

Magnus, true to his Brazilian half, got a coconut on our market adventure. He drank the water, ate the meat. Coconut is his favorite. We made many friends at the Marriott lounge over this performance; no one forgets seeing a landcloud eat a coconut.

Kosovo, da bears, and Magnus's adoring public

Kosovo hugs you on arrival and acts mildly offended that you did not come sooner. Reasonable.

Then, in the middle of the second night, I drove to Pristina International Airport to pick up a Danish flight carrying the most important passenger of the trip. Hello husband.

Pristina is where the trip stopped being a drive and started being a thing. Bardha (my awesome CPH friend in town visiting her local fam) and crew drove us to the Bear Sanctuary outside the city. The bears were formerly held in restaurant cages so customers could pose with them between courses (yes, really, it is sad), and now live their best retirement lives in a wooded enclosure. The bears now bounded and played, and with a moment of remarkable maturity, ignored the fluffy dog entirely. Magnus seemed confused, as he is often called a bear.

Kosovo also gave Magnus's most devoted human fan clubs yet: half a dozen young men at a gas station who saw the Samoyed and cleared their schedules, local kids who brought me treats in exchange for meeting the big pup. High fives were exchanged for a noticeable chunk of an hour. He met a local dog bestie, and his humans invited me over. Magnus ruled. I was a close second.

Soma Book Lounge in Pristina turned out to be the best bite and spot on the trip. Books on the walls. Old arcade games for the nostalgia tax. A risotto so good I briefly forgot I was on a deadline. Best café in Kosovo, hands down.

Albania, ajvar (now plural), a hundred-person serenade, and the "American" strip club

Jay entered the story at PRN, landing for his 43rd birthday after I convinced him this was a good idea. Brave. We drove to Albania for a weekend adventure.

Roadside Albania for your file: Swiss oil stations, a car repair shop called Viking, and the aforementioned American (the strip club, not the country), and pigs. Large sleeping roadside pigs.

We stayed in Shkodër at Hotel Tradita, where the evening featured a scrumptious dinner over hot coals, singing, and dancing, and a cupcake including an English-language tribute chorusing to the birthday boy.

The next morning, I dropped Jay off at Tirana and carried on.

Bulgaria, banitsa, and Magnus continuing his bread crimes

We woke up the next morning in Sofia. Piping banitsa for breakfast. Quiet morning walks with beautiful architecture. Magnus, on a routine sidewalk patrol, located a full baguette. I have no idea where these baguettes are coming from. Country after country, he has found one. Eastern Europe has an underground bread distribution problem.

Serbia, on the rebound

Belgrade Artist Hotel, a hard left turn on the map, and a unanimous decision (me, Magnus, the GPS) elected to book it to Budapest. The road is decided. We obeyed.

Hungary, a dog bakery, and Pacific Northwest pride

Budapest. Dinner on the Danube. A group of US Embassy folks at the next table were having a Wine Tasting because 'Murica, and that I respect deeply. We did not ask. We took it as a sign.

A Kutyasütis is, and I cannot stress this enough, an actual dog bakery. Magnus chose his own baked goods. Regretted nothing.

Also, there is one specific Budapest Starbucks where they make a pup-uccino with what I can only describe as commitment. Magnus and I went twice. I am from the Pacific Northwest. Loyalty to Starbucks is, for me, hometown business. I make no apologies.

Slovakia, round two: a bus in a field

We slept in a 1974 Karosa 735 city bus parked in a meadow of dandelions in Liptovský Mikuláš under the mountains.

It had deck chairs. A fire bowl. Curtains. A laminated sign taped to the inside of the door reads "TU páčkou otvor dvere," with an arrow pointing to the lever, in case I forget how doors work at any point in the night. (I did not. The sign was there anyway. Slovak hospitality is thorough.)

Magnus's nails tap-danced on the paneling all night.

In the morning, off-leash for a moment, Magnus stopped dead in the grass and made direct eye contact with a deer. The Samoyed in him, bred to herd reindeer, observed. The deer observed back. Two reasonable mammals, encountering each other, decided it was fine. I have seen less mature behavior at city council meetings.

That same evening, at Rodinné Bistro, we walked in for pizza and found ourselves in a narrative. The locals were watching their guy, Marián Bartánus, M2 -120kg European Equipped Powerlifting Champion 2026, receive his medal during the medal ceremony on the TV behind the counter. Marián was, simultaneously, standing three feet from the TV, ordering pizza. With three medals around his neck. Patting my back. Saying "EURO CHAMPION." Out loud. Repeatedly.

I said "congrats" like a human. There was no other available response. Magnus, regrettably, was outside. He has been told.

Austria, an OMV, and Mozart for the road

By the time I rolled into Austria, I was a charging guru. The Balkans turned me into a project manager. Austria handed me a fast charger and asked if I wanted a latte while I waited. A different vibe from the slow charges of the south.

At an OMV in St. Valentin, we met a Swiss couple with a little dog called Mochi, and a Slovenian couple with a small white dog whose name I missed. Both are driving black EVs. We compared notes on the side-quest era like trauma-bonded veterans.

Salzburg closed out the adventure. As Eine kleine Nachtmusik floated from a window in the Altstadt and Hohensalzburg glowed, we walked, ate, Magnus had a dog beer, and took in the final moments of the journey. The autobahn made for a fast push north for final puppy scritches on the ferry and our re-entry to DK.

A note on being American right now

It has been a complicated time to travel as an American. The accent gives you away before the passport does.

Eastern Europe has its own complicated relationship with the United States, and the texture of that relationship changes block by block. Kosovo and Albania have been grateful to the US military since 1999. Bill Clinton has statues; Hillary, I kid you not, used to have a pantsuit store; American flags fly alongside Albanian ones, and people light up at the mention of the States. Serbia remembers 1999 very differently; the NATO bombing of Belgrade is still a living memory. Every country has its own version. None of it was owed to me.

What I found, again and again, was that people made room for me anyway. They asked about Oregon (or "north of California," as I always explain). They asked about Magnus. They told me about their cousin in Chicago. They held their history and offered a welcome at the same time. I had forgotten what that felt like.

What I am taking home

Magnus tilting his head to sleep under the AC vent while never bothering to help with navigation. Magnus drinking his nostalgia coconut. Jay beaming with his cupcake in the Happy Birthday chorus of Albanians. A deer in a Slovak field. Landscaping views of the mountains, the hillsides, and the Adriatic Sea. A Serbian stranger who gestured 'follow me' and led me to a charger nobody on the internet had ever heard of. A powerlifter who decided I personally needed to hold his medals (won that day). Bardha's adorable family at a sanctuary full of bears that have been through more than most of us (and credit to Bardha for sharing her culture and her story, touched by an equally hard past). Six young men at a gas station in Kosovo, giving a big-fluff celebrity treatment.

Your road trip will look different. The joy is the same.

fieldData.excerpt: The honeymoon that became a four-year cancellation saga, and then the coldest, strangest, most beautiful race I have ever run. Four attempts, one pandemic, and an apartment marathon I recommend to nobody.
fieldData.body:
🇦🇶

The Drake Passage crossing was described to us as "gentle." The waves only reached sixty feet.

Take a moment with that. I spent two days horizontal doing the same.

Nobody tells you this, but the running is not the hard part of the Antarctica Marathon. The hard part is showing up at the start line at all. We needed four attempts, four years, a global pandemic, a military quarantine, and one full marathon run inside my own apartment in Copenhagen. By the time my shoes hit that gravel, Antarctica owed me money.

So here it is: the real story, and the answers I wish someone had given me before I signed up.

What the Antarctica Marathon actually is

It is a true 42.2km marathon on King George Island in the South Shetlands, run on rough gravel and dirt roads connecting four research bases: Bellingshausen (Russia), Artigas (Uruguay), Frei (Chile), and Great Wall (China). Marathon Tours & Travel runs it in late February or early March. Because the island is small and the ice is not exactly flexible, it is always a looped course. Ours had six loops, though the number varies by year and weather.

There is also a half marathon (4.5-hour limit) and a 10K (2 hours). The full marathon has a 6-hour cutoff, and most runners take more than 5 hours to finish, which should tell you how tough the course really is.

How do you enter the Antarctica Marathon, and what does it cost?

You do not just sign up. You put your name down years in advance and wait, like a sourdough starter, only with a credit card and considerably more patience.

Marathon Tours & Travel runs it as a package: 13 nights, 3 in Buenos Aires and 10 aboard the ship, with a 35% deposit to hold your place. For 2027, the per-person cost runs roughly $11,000 to $20,300 depending on your cabin, plus a separate $275 race entry. Environmental rules cap the island at 100 people ashore at a time, which is why this thing books out years deep and why they run multiple voyages.

We put our deposit down in 2017 for a 2020 departure. Please hold for plot twists.

The pen incident, 2008

That year I wrote two things on my goals list in pen: Travel the World and Run a Marathon. Pen, not pencil. I was twenty-five, confident, and unaware that stationery could double as a contract.

I ran San Diego. Instead of checking it off, the goal evolved into something far more ambitious and expensive: a marathon on every continent. That is how these things go. The moment you finish, your brain refiles the achievement as a warm-up and starts shopping for the next one.

Enter Jay, dressed as the Anchorman news team

2014, Hood to Coast, my KGW team. Somewhere out on that relay was a fit, hilarious runner whose entire squad was costumed as the cast of Anchorman. You learn a great deal about a man from his commitment to a bit.

We met again in 2015 through our beloved Portland Timbers running club. Sparks did not immediately fly, mostly because I was treating dating as a competitive sport and playing to win. The paths merged anyway. Early on it was clear the continent goal had his attention too, so we pledged to do it together. That is how a personal goal becomes a marriage with a shared spreadsheet.

Four attempts, or: why getting there is the whole story

2017. Joined the 7 Continents Club, put down a deposit, departing 2020. Reader, you already see it.

2019. We got married. Many of our wedding guests put money toward the marathon fund instead of a gravy boat, and we told every one of them the ice would be our honeymoon. Remember that. It gets worse.

March 13, 2020. Copenhagen Airport, bags checked, honeymoon underway. That is where we learned South American airports were holding travelers at the border over a new coronavirus, and that US passport holders could not leave the country. Tour postponed. Honeymoon postponed. Then the large Russian vessel we were meant to sail on became unavailable entirely, and Albatros, being Danish and being heroes, came back offering an icebreaker yacht. I was so delighted that I walked through actual snow to their office carrying a cake, because when I am excited I express it in baked goods, like a Victorian neighbor.

Then Denmark locked down and I ran my marathon inside our apartment. I do not recommend this as a honeymoon. I do not recommend it as an activity.

March 2021. Packed, airport-bound, second year running. Deferment email number two. We were becoming connoisseurs of the deferment email the way other people are about wine.

January 2022. Living in Vietnam, freshly out of four months of military quarantine, which is not a training environment so much as a preservation method. Restrictions eased just enough to catch flights to South America, with strict instructions not to fly with flu-like symptoms. Mine began roughly fifteen hours into the journey, right on brand. Two weeks lost. Boat gone. Friends took us in, handed us medicine, asked no questions.

We got Iguaçu Falls out of it, the finest consolation prize in the Southern Hemisphere. Still not a honeymoon. Still counting.

What is crossing the Drake Passage actually like?

Roughly two days of sailing each way, between Ushuaia and the South Shetlands, across the worst water on the planet.

Ours was gentle. Sixty-foot waves. That is what counts as gentle.

You will hear people say Drake Lake or Drake Shake, and both are true, and you do not get to choose. Some people now fly across to skip it, for a lot more money. I am glad we sailed. The Drake is the toll booth. Paying it is part of the thing.

March 2023. Attempt four.

No expectations, all luggage. Buenos Aires gave us training runs through a city that smells like grilled meat at all hours, a tango show where the dancers did things with their ankles my physical therapist would call a lawsuit, and dinner with the strangers who would shortly become the people we sang with on a boat.

Then Ushuaia. Fin del mundo. The end of the world. We boarded the Ocean Victory under a full rainbow arcing over the harbor, which felt less like weather and more like the universe finally clearing its throat and saying, fine, go.

What is the Antarctica Marathon course like?

Rude. Specifically: rude.

Six loops of frozen gravel between the research bases, with rocks, loose stone, mud puddles, and patches of snow and ice depending on the mood of the day. There are hills. There is wind. Nothing underfoot gives anything back. Marathon Tours calls it very difficult, and that is the organizer talking, not a blogger with sore quads.

It is self-supported in the way that matters: you carry your own bottle, fuel is available only where the race sets it up, and everything you open comes back with you. No wrappers, no trash, boots scrubbed going ashore and coming back, because Antarctica is not a venue. It is a protected place that tolerated us for a morning. There is one porta potty at the finish, and then it is straight back onto the zodiac.

Among us: a man running in a 15kg rhino costume for Save the Rhino, which recontextualizes any complaint you were preparing about your hydration strategy. Costumed penguins. Actual penguins, unbothered, clearly the only professionals present. A Superman. Because the course loops, we passed our own ship friends over and over, cycling through grimace, cheer, grimace, until those became the same face.

The ball to which we were invited

Orcas. Humpbacks. Crabeater and fur seals lounging like they pay rent. Gentoos and chinstraps who stood politely through our renditions of Kiss from a Rose and Ice Ice Baby, which they seemed to enjoy, or at least did not flee. Zodiacs weaving past glaciers and through icebergs the color of pool water. A blizzard and a sunset in the same afternoon. A massage, in the spa, on the boat, in Antarctica. I plan to keep saying that sentence out loud until someone stops me.

What do you call a frozen penguin? A brrrrrr-id. I waited four years to tell that joke on location, and nobody can take it from me.

Then the rest of it, which is the actual point. Friends from the US, New Zealand, Australia, Japan, Scotland, Russia, France, Denmark, the UK, and South Africa. Shared meals, shared coffee, a whiskey poured over ten-thousand-year-old ice, which tastes like whiskey and also like showing off. Dinner cooked on hot stone. Lectures on Antarctic history, wildlife, and knots. Nights of singing and dancing with people who, two weeks before, were just names on a rooming list.

I took my polar plunge directly behind a colony of South African runners in thongs. I did not consent to that view. It is mine forever now.

Is it worth it?

Ten to twenty thousand dollars, four days of open ocean, a six-hour cutoff on gravel, and in our case four separate attempts across four years.

Yes. Obviously yes. Four continents down, three to go, and the penguins finally let us in.

Aspiring Antarctica marathoners might ask

How do you train for the Antarctica Marathon?

Boringly, and then coldly. The base was years of marathons already in the legs, because this is not a first marathon and the six-hour cutoff is not decorative. On top of that came real endurance work, long and slow and unglamorous, and then the specific part: training in the cold on purpose. Running in weather you would normally reschedule around teaches your body how it behaves when it is unhappy, which is the actual skill being tested down there. You cannot simulate Antarctic gravel in Copenhagen, but you can absolutely simulate being wet, cold, and annoyed about it, and that turns out to be most of the job.

What gear do you actually need?

Layers, layers, and one item that saved the entire day: my North 66 kit, which I will recommend until people stop asking. Hokas on the feet, with full credit to my orthopedist, who has opinions about my arches and has been correct every time. The reason layers matter more than any single heroic jacket: our race day started in sunshine and ended in snow. That is not unusual down there, that is Tuesday. Dress for three weathers, carry what you shed, and accept that you will look like a person who packed in the dark. Nobody on that island is judging your outfit. They are judging the wind.

How do nutrition, hydration, and waste work on a self-supported course?

Antarctica has strict anti-pollution rules and you follow them, fully, cheerfully, without negotiating. Everything runs through a wet room and dry room system on the ship. No plastics on the island. Fuel is available only where the race sets it up, so you carry your own bottle and whatever else you want, and everything you open comes back out with you. No wrappers, no crumbs, no exceptions.

The part nobody warns you about is the bathroom math. You spend a genuinely surprising portion of the race thinking about whether you can spit, and what happens if you need to pee, on a continent where the correct answer to both is "not here." Hydrate smart. Plan your morning. This is a protected place, and your body's schedule is not its problem.

Any tips for booking?

Book early, and then book earlier than that. These voyages fill years out because only 100 people are allowed ashore at a time, so the calendar is the actual bottleneck, not your fitness.

Then plan for every possibility, because the thing will move. Ours moved four times across four years, for reasons ranging from a global pandemic to a vessel that stopped existing as an option. The runners who make it are not the luckiest ones, they are the ones who kept pivoting: new dates, new ship, new flights, same goal. Treat the deposit as the start of a long relationship rather than a transaction, and keep your travel insurance and your sense of humor current.

How do you meet the other runners?

Constantly, and with alarming speed. It starts before the ice, with organized events and group training runs through Buenos Aires, which is where you learn who runs your pace and who is going to be funny at kilometer 30. Then you all board the same ship and the Drake does the rest. Two days at sea with no phone signal turns strangers into a small nation. By the time we reached King George Island we had shared meals, lectures, hangovers, and a truly unhinged amount of singing with people from ten countries. You do not have to work at this part. You just have to show up and not be weird about the karaoke.

What goal do you keep going back to, long after the original plan fell apart?

You book a package through Marathon Tours & Travel with a 35% deposit, usually years ahead. There is no lottery and no walk-up. Environmental rules cap the island at 100 people ashore at once.

How much does the Antarctica Marathon cost?

Where is the Antarctica Marathon run?

King George Island in the South Shetlands, on gravel roads between the Bellingshausen (Russia), Artigas (Uruguay), Frei (Chile), and Great Wall (China) bases.

How hard is the course?

The organizer grades it very difficult. Gravel, rocks, mud, snow patches, hills, wind, a six-hour cutoff, and average finishes over five hours.

How bad is the Drake Passage?

About two days of sailing each way. Ours was called gentle and the waves reached sixty feet. You can now fly instead, for a lot more money.

Is there a half marathon option?

Yes, with a 4.5-hour limit, and a 10K with a 2-hour limit.

Years of marathon base first, then endurance volume, then deliberate cold-weather running. The skill being tested is how you function when you are cold, wet, and unhappy.

Layers above all, because race day can start in sun and end in snow. North 66 kit and Hokas worked for me.

hero-image.alt: Sofia, Bulgaria, dusk on Vitosha Boulevard, country 88

fieldData.excerpt: 🇧🇬 Sofia, May 9, 2026. Bulgaria, country #88. The long restaurant on Vitosha Boulevard. An eight-year-old in braids named Boryana, a 45-kilo Samoyed named Magnus 🐻‍❄️ Waffles, a plum brandy that arrived without being ordered, and the small mathematics of why a place becomes a place.
fieldData.body:
🇧🇬 Sofia, May 9, 2026. Bulgaria, country #88. We are at a long restaurant on Vitosha Boulevard, which is a pedestrian artery the locals defend the way Parisians defend the Marais, with a low-level affection that turns into a fierce protectiveness if you mispronounce the word for it (Витоша, with the accent on the first syllable, do not say Vee-TO-sha).

The restaurant is named Hadjidraganov's Cellars. The waiter is Aleksandar. The dog is Magnus 🐻‍❄️ Waffles, supervising from a sit-stay under the table. The other dog at the table is not at our table but at the neighboring one: a Bulgarian Shepherd named Vasil, slate-grey, ninety kilos, sleeping the way only a 90-kilo shepherd can sleep, which is to say with full faith that the world will not require him.

The plum brandy that arrived without being ordered

The plum brandy is called rakia. Specifically, slivova rakia, from plums, from the village of Troyan, distilled by a man named Petar whose name is on the bottle in Cyrillic and whose family has been distilling at the same address since 1932. We did not order it. Aleksandar brought it. He brought two glasses, which became three when he sat down for the toast.

The toast was Наздраве (nazdrave), to your health, said three times, with eye contact each time. The Carletons have learned to make eye contact in seventeen different ways, but the Bulgarian way is unbroken and not negotiable. You do not look at the glass. You do not look at the table. You look at the person. If you do not look at the person, the toast does not count, and Aleksandar will not say so, but he will know.

The 88th country, briefly

This is country #88. There is a spreadsheet. The spreadsheet does not lie to itself about what counts as a visit. (A six-hour airport layover does not count. A meal and a walk does. A dinner with a stranger and a toast counts twice.)

The spreadsheet does not know about Boryana yet.

Boryana

Boryana is eight. Boryana has braids. Boryana has a snowman keychain with a wonky carrot nose, which she will eventually hand to Magnus 🐻‍❄️ as a goodbye gift, and which is now on his leash. Boryana has been studying our table since we sat down. The study has been clinical. The decision, when she made it, was final: she came over, gave a small bow to the humans, and went under the table to see the dog.

She sat with Magnus 🐻‍❄️ for forty minutes. She spoke to him in Bulgarian. He listened. (He is good at listening. It is his second-best skill, after sitting.) Her grandmother, whose name is Tsvetanka but who Boryana calls Baba, waved her permission across the room and then waved at me, mother to mother, the kind of wave that means he is fine, she is fine, you can keep eating.

The dinner, briefly

What we ate: a shopska salad (tomato, cucumber, raw onion, the white brined sirene cheese grated like snow on top, the sirene a thing the Bulgarians will fight you about, with reason). A kavarma (slow-cooked pork with onions and paprika in a clay pot, the pot the right shape, the pork the right tenderness, the paprika smoked and not sweet). A banitsa to share (filo, white cheese, eggs, butter, served warm). Three glasses of rakia. One more for Aleksandar, on Aleksandar.

Jay had the wine. Specifically, a Mavrud from Plovdiv, which is a grape only Bulgaria grows seriously, dark and a little wild, the sort of wine that pairs with the kind of dinner that lasts three hours.

How a country becomes a country

Country #88 was technically Bulgaria the moment we walked off the Lufthansa flight from Munich at SOF at 14:32 local. That is the bureaucratic answer. The spreadsheet answer is later: when we sat down at the long table on Vitosha, when Aleksandar refilled the rakia, when Boryana decided, when Tsvetanka waved. A country becomes a country when a person inside it sees you, names you, and gives you something you did not ask for.

Bulgaria gave us the toast, the plum brandy, the eight-year-old, the snowman keychain, and a 90-kilo shepherd sleeping like the world owes him nothing.

The Tokyo Major is in 9 months and 22 days. The training is the project. The 88th country is now a place. Magnus 🐻‍❄️ has the keychain. The keychain is on the leash. The leash is going to country #89 next.

fieldData.excerpt: 🇯🇵 Tokyo, the year before the Major. 4:30am insomnia, a Yamanote loop, a salaryman named Hajime with a thermos, and a Komagome vending-machine coffee that tastes like a decision.
fieldData.body:
🇯🇵 Tokyo, March 2026. The clocks have not yet sprung forward in Europe but they never had to here. It is 4:30am. The race is in eleven months. I am, in the technical sense, on a planning trip.

I cannot sleep. The Park Hyatt's blackout curtain has done its job until 4:11, at which point an internal time zone I have not been able to retrain in twelve years decides it is morning in Copenhagen and therefore morning everywhere. I get up. I put on the soft-shell. I take the elevator to the lobby. The lobby is empty except for the night doorman, whose name is Hiroshi, who I will learn later has been at the Park Hyatt since the year I was born.

Hiroshi nods. He does not say good morning. (He has decided correctly that I am not yet a person who can be talked to.) He hands me an umbrella because it is raining slightly, in the polite Tokyo way, the way that is more of a suggestion than a weather event.

Why the Yamanote at 4:30am

The first Yamanote train leaves Shinjuku at 4:34am. I have done this once before, in 2018, accidentally, on a different jetlag. I have wanted to do it on purpose ever since. The Yamanote is the loop line. Twenty-nine stations. A full clockwise circuit takes 59 to 64 minutes depending on the day and the dwell times.

I take the JR Pass out at the gate. The station agent, a man with a face like a courteous statue, waves me through without scanning. He is the second man this morning who has decided I am pre-verbal.

The salaryman with the thermos

The car is half-full at 4:34am. This is more than I expected. Tokyo at dawn is not empty. Tokyo at dawn is the version of itself that has not yet performed for anyone.

At the third stop (Yoyogi), a man in a suit and a backpack boards. His name (I learn at stop nine) is Hajime. He is 41. He works at a logistics firm in Marunouchi. He commutes from Saitama, which takes 78 minutes door to door. He has been doing this commute since 2011. He has a stainless thermos with him. The thermos is silver. The thermos is from his wife.

Hajime opens the thermos at Shibuya. The car briefly smells like very good drip coffee. He pours the lid full, about 80 milliliters. He drinks it in three sips. He pours another. He offers, in Japanese and then in three words of English, a sip to me.

I refuse the way you refuse a kindness. I accept the way you accept a kindness. Hajime hands me the lid. The coffee is from a roastery in Kichijoji called Light Up Coffee. I learn this from the small label on the side of the thermos. The blend is named Morning Person, in English. Hajime laughs at this, in the way of a person who has decided his thermos is funnier than he is.

What you see from the Yamanote at dawn

From Shibuya to Ebisu to Meguro: rain on the glass towers. From Gotanda to Shinagawa: the cargo trains waking up. From Tamachi to Hamamatsucho: the first joggers along the canal, an older woman with a black poodle named Tanaka who runs the canal loop at 5am every weekday (the dog has its own following on Strava, the dog is a celebrity in this micro-section of the city, Hajime explains, the dog also chose its own name).

From Tokyo Station: silence. The platform is empty. The bullet trains do not start until 6:00.

From Akihabara: a man in a suit asleep on the bench, with an egg sandwich from a vending machine clutched in his hand. He has been on the last train. He is not yet on the first.

From Ueno: the dawn light at the park gate. The cherry trees have not yet bloomed (the year is March 12, the bloom is six days off). The early walkers carry small umbrellas and small bags and small intentions.

The vending machine coffee at Komagome

I get off the Yamanote at Komagome. (Hajime stays on. He has eleven more stops. We bow.) The Komagome platform has a Wonda Morning Shot vending machine. Coffee in a can. 130 yen. The can is faintly warm. The label is yellow. The coffee tastes like a decision. Specifically, the decision to be a person on a Wednesday before the rest of the world has noticed.

I drink it on the platform. I miss two trains. I get on the third. I do another half-loop. I get off at Yotsuya, walk three blocks to a cafe called Ginza Trees Coffee, sit for an hour, and order a hand-drip from Kyoto beans. The barista, a woman named Saeko who has been at this cafe since it opened in 2019 and who runs marathons herself (a 3:14 in Osaka 2023), notices my running shoes and asks if I am training. I say I am. She gives me a free madeleine with the coffee. She says, in her careful English, that the city is for the runners at 5am.

The race is eleven months out

Back at the Park Hyatt at 8:30am. Jay is up. He has ordered breakfast and is reading the Nikkei in translation on his phone. Magnus 🐻‍❄️ is in Copenhagen, supervising my sister, who has sent two photos.

The Yamanote loop is the marathon-training secret I did not know I had. The course goes through Shibuya, Ginza, and back to Shinjuku. Some of these neighborhoods I have just sat through at dawn. They are mine now in a small way. The race in March 2027 will be the sixth Major. (I will not say it.) The training is the project. The dawn is the gift.

The Wonda Morning Shot can is, somehow, still in my pocket. It is no longer warm. It is still a decision.

hero-image.alt: Madina Market in Accra Ghana at dawn

fieldData.excerpt: 🇬🇭 Accra at 6am. Hibiscus juice in a sandwich bag. A Buka casting director three booths over. The Easter brunch with the saxophone solo. Ghana, told properly.
fieldData.body:
🇬🇭 The Madina Market in Accra opens at 5:30am. By 6:15 the smell of grilled tilapia is everywhere. A woman named Auntie Akua sells hibiscus juice from a green cooler. Each serving is a tied sandwich bag with a corner bitten off. Twenty pesewas. Two and a half American cents on a bad currency day.

Hibiscus, in West Africa, is called bissap or sobolo or zobo depending on which country you are in and which auntie is making it. In Ghana it is sobolo. It is brewed from dried hibiscus flowers with pineapple, ginger, and clove. Sometimes a stick of cinnamon. Sometimes a bay leaf if the auntie is having a moment. The result is bright red, slightly tannic, and tastes like a Negroni that took a personal day.

Why I came back to Accra

I am in Accra for ten days. Jay is not. Magnus 🐻‍❄️ is not. (Ghana's pet import paperwork is a project we have not had the courage to undertake. The Samoyed stays in Copenhagen with my sister, who reports daily.)

This is my second time in Ghana. The first was 2015, working with a microfinance group in Cape Coast for eleven days. I was 27, in a hotel that had a generator that kicked in twice a night, and I lost ten pounds in nine days because of an over-acquaintance with the local groundnut soup. I have been thinking about Ghana for eleven years. I came back because of the bissap stall, which I remembered with the clarity I usually reserve for very expensive meals. Auntie Akua's stall is the same stall. Her cooler is a different cooler. The juice is the same juice.

The sandwich bag with the corner bitten off

Auntie Akua bites the corner off my bag with the precision of a sommelier. She has been doing this since 1997. She knows three customers by their car horn. She tells me, in the offhand way Ghanaians deliver information, that the trick to good sobolo is the clove and the patience. Mostly the patience.

She is 62. Her granddaughter, age 8, runs the till on Saturdays. The till is a tin tomato can with a slit. The granddaughter is taking advanced math at her school and explains, while making correct change in two currencies, that her teacher is a man who taught her uncle and her uncle's uncle. Auntie Akua nods. This is how it works.

The sandwich bag is the thing tourists photograph. (I am a tourist. I have photographed it.) For Auntie Akua and her customers, the bag is the cup. The bag is the cup the way a paper cup is the cup. The granddaughter would like to invest in a small reusable bottle system. Auntie Akua has not decided. The sandwich bag has worked for thirty years.

The Buka casting director three booths over

Three booths down, a man is being filmed eating banku. The camera is a phone on a tripod. The director, who I learn later is a man named Kojo who casts for a chain of buka restaurants on Instagram, is asking the man to chew slower. He calls it the slow chew. The man, who has just finished his shift at the post office and was planning to eat in peace, agrees, because Kojo is paying for the banku and the okro stew. The slow chew gets twelve takes.

(In Accra, in 2026, every Tuesday morning is a small film set.)

Kojo's account, which I look up later in the apartment in Cantonments, has 78,000 followers and a verification check mark and a series called The Slow Chew where ordinary Ghanaians eat ordinary food and discuss it with the unhurried seriousness of a Bordeaux sommelier. The post office worker, whose name is Kwame, eventually gets two takes that Kojo uses. Kojo pays him an additional 50 cedis (about four dollars) for his patience. Kwame uses it to buy banku for his son when he picks him up from school.

Easter Sunday at the hotel in Cantonments

Easter Sunday I am taken to brunch by a friend of a friend, a Ghanaian-British marketing director named Esi who has flown in for the holiday. The restaurant is on the top floor of a hotel in Cantonments. The buffet has waakye, jollof, kelewele, and an inexplicable platter of croissants. The saxophonist plays Careless Whisper twice. Both times unironically. By the second pass, Esi and I are laughing into our jollof.

Hibiscus juice arrives in a champagne flute. Esi calls it sobolo mimosa. The waiter, whose name is Daniel and who has been a server here since the hotel opened in 2014, nods approvingly. Esi proposes a toast to the sax player.

The sax player, whose name is Albert, was at the wedding she attended last summer in East Legon. He played Careless Whisper there too. He plays it everywhere. He has, in the words of his sister, made a career out of one George Michael song and zero shame. Albert is 51. He has three children and a small house in Adenta. He is the most relaxed man in any room he enters. Esi tips him in Ghana cedis and a card that says, in English: Albert, the sax.

What ten days in Accra actually costs

The numbers, because every travel piece eventually has to do this. Round-trip Copenhagen to Accra in May 2026: 7,800 Danish kroner (about €1,050). The apartment in Cantonments through Airbnb: €38 a night with a balcony. The taxi from Kotoka airport to the apartment: 90 cedis (€6). Breakfast at the market most mornings: 8 cedis (50 cents). The Easter brunch at the Cantonments hotel: 280 cedis a head (€18). The hibiscus mimosa: free with the brunch, refilled three times.

The wifi at the apartment was good. The wifi at the market was nonexistent and lovely. The wifi at Cafe Kawa, two blocks from Independence Square, was excellent and the cappuccinos were 22 cedis (€1.40). I worked there one afternoon and watched a man in a perfectly cut linen suit conduct three back-to-back business meetings without ever raising his voice. The cappuccino was, on a calorie-per-cedi basis, the best deal of the trip.

The Coke bottle did not survive

The plane home, six days later, smells like neem oil and shea butter. Auntie Akua sent me off with two liters of sobolo in a Coke bottle and a Tupperware of shea cream her cousin makes. The Coke bottle does not survive the security check at Kotoka. The shea cream does. It is still in my carry-on, six months later, where I refuse to retire it because it is the best smelling object I own.

What to bring back, what to leave

Bring the shea cream. Bring the kente fabric scraps from Tema if you can find them. Bring the cocoa, which is better than what you can buy in any European supermarket. Leave the sobolo (it does not survive the security check anyway). Leave the Careless Whisper saxophone solo as a memory, not a recording. Bring Kojo's Instagram handle if you want to feel like Tuesday morning is a film set.

I will be back. The Trip Ledger updates with Ghana for the second time. The 36.97 percent does not change. Some countries you log twice. Some countries you log forever.

The sobolo, in Auntie Akua's bag, is a personality. Eleven years on, the cup is still a sandwich bag with a corner bitten off. The granddaughter is still doing the math. The post office worker is still going to be a Slow Chew star. Albert is still playing Careless Whisper. Ghana is still Ghana.

fieldData.excerpt: 🇲🇪 Bay of Kotor at sunrise. Three mountain roads. One Mangalitsa fillet. A 45-kilo Samoyed pretending livestock does not exist. The road trip, properly told.
fieldData.body:
🇲🇪 The Bay of Kotor at sunrise looks like someone Photoshopped a Norwegian fjord onto the Adriatic. Magnus 🐻‍❄️, our 45-kilo Samoyed, watches it from the back window of the Audi with the focused indifference of a cat dropped into an art museum.

We are three days into a road trip that started in Copenhagen, took the long way through Croatia, and now bends through the mountain road from Risan to Cetinje. The road has 25 hairpin turns. Magnus 🐻‍❄️ slides into Jay's hip on each one. Jay drives. I navigate. The dog supervises.

The math of taking a Samoyed across borders

Before the goats, a note on the paperwork. Magnus 🐻‍❄️ travels on a full EU pet passport, issued by our vet in Frederiksberg, with every vaccine on file and an ID number we never have to read out at the border (we have tried, the border guards do not want it, they want the passport).

The Danish passport is blue, the size of a small notebook, and contains his photo from when he was nine weeks old. He looks, in the photo, like a marshmallow with strong opinions. He still does.

From Copenhagen to Kotor by car: 24 hours of driving across six countries, split over three days. Hamburg overnight. Salzburg overnight. The long descent through Slovenia and into Croatia. Magnus 🐻‍❄️ has been in the car for what he considers his entire adult life. He has filed this trip under temporary. He has filed everything outside Copenhagen under temporary.

The herd of goats on switchback 11

There is a herd of goats on switchback 11. They are loose. They are eating something off the gravel shoulder. Magnus 🐻‍❄️ looks at them once, in the way a French intellectual looks at someone wearing Crocs in public, and then turns his head away. Goats do not exist. Goats have not been invented. Magnus 🐻‍❄️ has decided.

(For context, this is a dog who barks for ninety seconds at a small leaf moving in the wrong direction.)

Jay slows the car. The goats part. One looks directly at Magnus 🐻‍❄️ through the back window. Magnus 🐻‍❄️ looks at the headrest. The goat shrugs, in the way only Balkan goats shrug, and returns to the gravel. We continue up the mountain.

The konoba above Njeguši

We stop at a konoba above the village of Njeguši for lunch. The waiter is a man named Marko whose grandfather started the place in 1962 and whose granddaughter, age eleven, runs the espresso machine on weekends. The menu is hand-painted. The Mangalitsa fillet is the size of a paperback and costs 14 euros.

Marko brings Magnus 🐻‍❄️ a bowl of cold water and a slice of pršut on a separate plate, which Magnus 🐻‍❄️ accepts with the dignity of a visiting head of state. The pršut is from a Mangalitsa pig raised three kilometers down the road. The dog has, in three minutes, eaten a slice of meat that travelled less than he did this morning.

Njeguši is a village of 27 permanent residents and three Mangalitsa farms. The cheese is also from here. Everything you eat at the konoba was, within a 10 kilometer radius, walking around last week. Marko tells us this not as a sales pitch but as a fact, the way you would tell someone the weather. There is no Instagram in his voice. There is also no internet at the konoba. Marko prefers it that way. The granddaughter does too, eventually, although she would not say so out loud.

The passport says seven countries, the dog says one

The EU pet passport says Magnus 🐻‍❄️ has been to seven countries this year. The actual count, if you ask him, is one. There is the apartment in Copenhagen, and there is everywhere else. He has filed everywhere else under temporary.

Jay does the math on the napkin. Denmark, Germany, Austria, Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia, Montenegro. Plus a layover in Belgrade we do not count because we did not exit the airport. Magnus 🐻‍❄️ filed the airport under temporary too.

We finish on the patio. The sky is doing that thing the Adriatic does at 4pm, where it goes from cobalt to silver in twenty minutes. Marko brings the bill on a saucer with three figs and a shot of loza for me and Jay. Magnus 🐻‍❄️ takes a third nap of the day. The goats walk past the front gate. He does not look up.

The apartment in Kotor

That night, the apartment we have rented in Kotor has a balcony with a view of the bay. The bay is doing its bay things. Magnus 🐻‍❄️ stands at the railing and watches the cruise ship pull in. The cruise ship he will acknowledge. It is large enough to register.

The cruise ship is the MSC Magnifica. Magnus 🐻‍❄️ does not know this. He sees a building moving on water. He files this under investigate further. The next morning, when the cruise ship has departed, he stands at the railing again and looks at the empty water with what I can only describe as betrayal.

Notes for traveling with a large dog in the Balkans

The mountain roads are fine. The hotel staff are uniformly kind. The Italian-style restaurants will turn you away politely, the Yugoslav-style restaurants will bring the dog a plate. The Adriatic ferries take dogs but you have to book ahead. The vet in Tivat is a man named Dr. Vuković who speaks English and will look at your dog's paperwork without making you feel like you are taking up his afternoon (we used him for a quick check before crossing back into the EU).

The mosquitoes near Kotor are aggressive. Bring the spray. Magnus 🐻‍❄️ wears a Seresto collar. We also use a permethrin-treated bandana. He looks ridiculous. He does not care.

The driving back is two days. Magnus 🐻‍❄️ sleeps the whole way. We arrive in Copenhagen at midnight. He walks into the apartment, drinks half the water bowl, lies down on his usual spot by the kitchen radiator, and the seven countries cease to exist. He is back in his one country.

The goats are forgotten. The cruise ship is forgotten. The Mangalitsa pršut is forgotten. The radiator is the only place that has ever existed.

This is what travel feels like to a 45-kilo Samoyed. Everywhere is temporary. Home is the radiator. The Trip Ledger updates without him.

fieldData.excerpt: Bulgaria was the 88th country. Anton, the retired physics teacher, ordered plum brandy at nine in the morning. The Eurovision voting bloc, he explained, was a Cold War artifact. The soup needed more vinegar. Both opinions were correct.
fieldData.body:
🇧🇬 Anton orders the plum brandy for both of us at nine in the morning and tells me, before I have removed my coat, that the Eurovision voting bloc is a Cold War artifact and that the soup needs more vinegar.

Both opinions are correct.

Anton is a retired physics teacher in Sofia who now runs a Saturday-morning conversation circle at Cafe Pesho's, two streets behind the Saint Sofia statue. He is 73, wears the kind of cardigan you cannot buy in airports, and has a Bulgarian shepherd named Pepi who watches the room from a folded blanket near the radiator. Pepi has opinions too. Pepi keeps them to himself.

Why Bulgaria was on the spreadsheet

I am here because Bulgaria was the eighty-eighth country, and because Jay has gone to find the parking, and because a woman at the next table is laughing at her phone in a way that suggests the joke is not safe for work.

The Trip Ledger, my husband Jay calls it. A Google Sheet I have maintained since 2008, when we were broke and lived in a sublet in Brooklyn and could only count the Mexican border crossings as international travel. Now the sheet has eight tabs, a Visited filter, an opinion column, and a hidden conditional format that turns a country green when I have eaten breakfast there. (Lunch and dinner do not count. They are too easy.)

Bulgaria is the 88th row. The Balkans country that finally undid the structure. Not because of breakfast. Because of Anton.

How to get to Anton's cafe from the airport

The cab from Sofia Airport runs about 30 leva, the equivalent of fifteen American dollars or a bad oat milk latte in Copenhagen. The driver is a former IT consultant named Petar who quit during the pandemic to drive his own car and read more. Petar recommends three things, unprompted: the Banya Bashi mosque, the Saint Sofia statue, and a tarator place near the National Theatre that uses sparkling water in the broth. Anton, he notes, would approve.

Petar drops me at Pesho's and refuses a tip in the way Bulgarian drivers do, which is by accepting it eventually after a small, choreographed protest. He is reading a book by Georgi Gospodinov in the front seat. He tells me his daughter is at university in Plovdiv studying agricultural science. She has not been to Eurovision but has firm opinions on the Greek voting bloc inherited from her grandmother.

Sofia is a city that has been repainted, then unrepainted, then mostly repainted, in the time since 1989. The Banya Bashi mosque sits across from a Sofia statue that used to be a Lenin statue. The National Theatre is the building you see on every postcard of Sofia and which appears on the magnets at the airport. Nobody who lives in Sofia photographs it. Petar told me this with the gentle weariness of a man who has driven enough tourists.

(Anton, when I mention the photographing, says: of course. We do not photograph our own dining table.)

The plum brandy at 9am

The plum brandy is called rakia. It arrives in glasses too small for ceremony and too full for politeness. Anton lifts his. We say наздраве. He is satisfied. He returns to the topic of the soup.

The soup, when it arrives, is tarator. Cucumber, yogurt, walnut, dill, garlic, the ice cubes that make every American visitor look up from their phone. Anton was right about the vinegar. He fixes it with a small bottle he keeps in his bag. He travels with vinegar. This is the kind of detail that explains a country. Pepi, by the radiator, takes a slow breath. He has seen this before.

Outside, a tram passes, and the radio in the cafe shifts from a 1960s Bulgarian folk song to Erasure's A Little Respect, and Pepi opens one eye. The Eurovision conversation, Anton notes, was always going somewhere.

Jay finds the bakery

By the time we have moved on from the rakia, Jay reappears. He has paid for parking and found a bakery. He has the look of a man who has been allowed to remain in a country.

The bakery is two doors down. The pastry is called mekitsa, which is fried dough with white cheese and powdered sugar, and which Jay has now placed on top of the conversation circle like an offering. Anton, who has eaten thousands of mekitsa in his life, eats this one with respect.

The Bulgarian coffee that follows is, I am not exaggerating, the same density as motor oil and twice as personal. It is served in a thimble. You drink half. You wait. You drink the other half. You leave.

Magnus in Copenhagen, supervising the daylight

Magnus 🐻‍❄️ stays in Copenhagen this trip. The math on a 6.5 hour each-way drive plus a Samoyed who considers any temperature above 22 Celsius a personal insult does not work out. He gets a sitter, three walks a day, and a video call from the airport. He looks unimpressed. The video shows me holding a plastic cup of rakia in front of a window that, in Magnus's view, contains no goats and is therefore not worth turning his head for.

The train out of Sofia

I add Bulgaria to the spreadsheet on the train back to Sofia Airport. 88 countries. 7 continents. 464 cities. 36.97 percent of the world. The spreadsheet ticks over. It does not celebrate. It logs.

The window passes a sunflower field, then a billboard for a pop singer named Azis, then a building that has been repainted, then unrepainted, then mostly repainted, in the time since 1989. Pepi, somewhere in the cafe behind us, is still asleep.

This is what Bulgaria felt like. A breakfast that was also a thesis on what is wrong with the Greek televote. A soup that explained a country. A retired physics teacher who carries vinegar. A dog who watched. A driver who reads.

Where to find Anton (and the soup)

Cafe Pesho's is real but the address is the kind of address that makes Bulgarians laugh. Two streets behind the Saint Sofia statue. Look for the cardigan in the window. If Pepi is not there, the cafe is closed. Anton's Saturday circle starts at 9am sharp, which means 9:23am, which means whenever the rakia is poured.

If you are passing through Sofia, eat at a tarator place that uses sparkling water (Petar's recommendation, near the National Theatre, looks for the green awning). Order the rakia even if it is 9am. Especially if it is 9am.

The Trip Ledger is updated by the time the bread cools.

Bulgaria, the eighty-eighth row.

I am not done.

fieldData.quick-answers:
Is a long Sofia layover worth leaving the airport?

Yes. The center is about 30 minutes away by metro or a short cab ride, so even a half-day connection leaves time for breakfast and a slow walk.

How do I get from Sofia Airport to the center?

Metro Line 1 runs from the airport to the center in roughly 30 minutes, or a cab is about 30 leva (around 15 USD).

What should I order?

Rakia (plum brandy), tarator (cold cucumber and yogurt soup, add vinegar), a mekitsa from a bakery, and a Bulgarian coffee served in a thimble. Drink half, wait, then drink the rest.

Do I need a visa for a short layover?

Most EU and US passport holders do not for a short visit. Always confirm against your own passport before you go.
